A Swarm config cannot change, so its name carries the first 12 hex digits of the SHA-256 of its file: if you edit a script, rename its config the same way (sha256sum <file> | cut -c1-12).

Review these settings first (Resource Classes has the details):

Setting Default Change it to
Service name linux-default Your resource class name
image cimg/base:2026.10 Your image, pinned by digest (Images)
deploy.replicas 2 The number of concurrent jobs you need
deploy.resources 2 CPUs and 4 GB The size of one runner. Limits and reservations are equal
placement.constraints node.platform.os == linux Add architecture or zone constraints
x-distributor-env An exact runner version (3.1.13 in this release) with the SHA-256 values of its tarballs, major version 3, a check every 24 hours Nothing for a first run. A newer pin, a floating version or a mirror are variables of docker stack deploy (Upgrade the runner on Linux)

The optional classes are add-on files in deploy/. Add each with another -c flag, and pass the same list on every deploy (how the files merge). Each needs its own resource class and secret <service>-token.

File Services Purpose
classes-extra.yaml linux-java, linux-hardened Examples: an image swap, and a class without sudo. Reserves 6 more CPUs and 12 GB (Define a class)
docker-build.yaml linux-docker-build Builds images with the host engine. Needs a labeled worker (Docker Builds)
microvm.yaml linux-microvm, linux-microvm-docker, microvm-dns Each job in a Kata Containers microVM. Needs KVM (MicroVM jobs)
persistent.yaml linux-persistent A long-lived runner. Needs the node name edited in the file (Persistent mode)
ssh-rerun.yaml linux-default-ssh Rerun job with SSH. Publishes port 54782 (Rerun job with SSH)

An add-on file repeats the common settings of runners.yaml (YAML anchors do not cross files), so it also loads alone. Change a common setting, such as stop_grace_period or the logging options, in every file that you use.

6. Deploy the stack

Deploy your copy from step 5. The command returns before the replicas run, because docker stack deploy does not wait.

docker stack deploy -c deploy/runners.yaml runners

To add optional classes, pass your copies with more -c flags, and pass the same list on every later deploy:

docker stack deploy -c deploy/runners.yaml -c deploy/persistent.yaml runners

This is the whole install. The service runner-distributor starts on every Linux node, also on a node that joins later (not on a microVM node: its classes download their own runner). It downloads the runner version the stack file pins (the newest that CI tests), checks its SHA-256 against the values the stack file carries, and puts it in the volume runner-bin of the node. The service token-proxy pulls its image from Docker Hub. A runner container that starts first waits up to 120 seconds for the runner.

Other distributor settings, such as a floating version like 3.1 (weaker: the distributor trusts the manifest and ignores the default SHA-256 list), are variables of this command. sudo drops the environment: write sudo env MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION=3.1 docker stack deploy ... (Upgrade the runner on Linux).

Verify the deployment

  1. List the services. Each shows the running and desired replicas.

    docker stack services runners
    ID NAME MODE REPLICAS IMAGE
... runners_linux-default replicated 2/2 cimg/base:2026.10
... runners_runner-distributor global 1/1 alpine:3
... runners_token-proxy replicated 1/1 ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy:...

    The distributor has one task for each Linux node (a microVM node has none): 1/1 on one node, 3/3 on three.

  2. Check the tasks. A task in the Running state is a runner that polls CircleCI.

    docker service ps runners_linux-default

  3. Check that the distributor installed the runner. Its log has a line such as runner-distributor: [ ok ] current -> versions/3.1.13: circleci-runner 3.1.13 linux/amd64 for each node (See what runs).

    docker service logs --tail 20 runners_runner-distributor

  4. Check that the runners connected. Each replica is listed as online, named <node hostname>-<service>-<slot> (for example node1-linux-default-1). The web app shows the same under Runners.

    circleci runner instance list --org <org> --resource-class <namespace>/linux-default

  5. Run a job with examples/linux-hello.yml (the quickstart shows it), twice. After each job, Swarm shows a new task for the slot. The job clean-check in examples/linux-jobs.yml fails if anything from an earlier job is still present.

Optional: use the setup helper

linux/setup.sh runs the steps above with checks. It never prints the token, every step is idempotent, and it needs bash 4.4 or later. It installs nothing on a node: the service runner-distributor installs the runner.

Step Effect
--check Preflight: Linux on amd64, arm64, ppc64le or s390x, Docker running and 24 or later, Swarm state, NTP
--swarm-init Runs docker swarm init on the loopback address unless Swarm is active, and sets the task history limit to 2
--secret <service> Creates the secret <service>-token from a token read on stdin
--deploy Runs docker stack deploy with each --stack-file. Without one it deploys the shipped linux/stack/runners.yaml, so pass your copy from step 5. It warns when MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE is not pinned by digest

With no step it runs --check. Steps run in the order of the table. Options are --stack-file (repeatable) and --stack-name. Each run ends with Next: and the steps still to do, or Check: and the commands that show the runners start.

sudo linux/setup.sh --check --swarm-init
sudo linux/setup.sh --secret linux-default
printf %s machine-runner-swarm-placeholder | sudo linux/setup.sh --secret runner-placeholder
sudo linux/setup.sh --deploy --stack-file deploy/runners.yaml
  • --secret asks for the token with a hidden prompt. To script it, pipe the token (printf %s "$TOKEN" | sudo linux/setup.sh --secret linux-default). Several --secret values need a terminal. A token has only letters, digits, ., _ and -, and an existing secret stays unchanged (Rotate a runner token). Create a secret for every service you deploy.
  • The helper does not label nodes. For a docker-build class, run docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.docker-build=true <worker node>.
  • The distributor reads MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION, MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_MAJOR, MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_CHECK_INTERVAL, MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_DOWNLOAD_BASE_URL and MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_SHA256 from the environment of --deploy, and the token proxy reads MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_*. sudo drops the environment: use sudo env VAR=value linux/setup.sh --deploy (Upgrade the runner on Linux).

Upgrade

The nodes keep the runner version that the stack file pins until you change it: Upgrade the runner and images covers versions, images and rollback.

A new release of this repository changes the shipped stack files, and your copy deploy/ is not updated by itself. To merge:

  1. Read the notes of the release and the changelog: entries marked [BREAKING] say what to change. This is a 0.x project, so a minor release can change the files.

  2. Verify and unpack the new release beside the old one (Verify a release). The old directory is the base of the merge (for a cloned tag, use git worktree or a second clone).

  3. See what changed between the two releases.

    diff -ru "machine-runner-swarm-${old}/linux/stack" "machine-runner-swarm-${new}/linux/stack"

  4. Merge each file that differs into your copy. The command edits the file in place, marks conflicts with <<<<<<< lines, and exits with the number of conflicts.

    git merge-file deploy/runners.yaml \
 "machine-runner-swarm-${old}/linux/stack/runners.yaml" \
 "machine-runner-swarm-${new}/linux/stack/runners.yaml"

    Repeat for the other files you copied. Take the entrypoint and the distributor script of the new release unless you edited them, and rename their Swarm configs as Upgrade to a new release of this repository says.

  5. Check deploy.replicas, image, deploy.placement.constraints and deploy.resources, the runner version pin with its SHA-256 values (a release changes them together), and the token proxy image (a release names it by digest).

  6. Check the result.

    docker stack config -c deploy/runners.yaml > /dev/null

  7. Deploy with the same list of -c files as before.

    docker stack deploy -c deploy/runners.yaml runners

Swarm replaces the token proxy and updates the runner services one replica at a time. While the proxy is replaced, no new job is claimed, and every runner that had already claimed stays refused (Restart the proxy). To roll back, deploy the previous copy.

Stop and uninstall

Refer to Uninstall.

Troubleshooting

Refer to Troubleshooting. The most common problems on a first install are a missing secret, a node whose distributor cannot download the runner, and a task that stays pending because no node matches its constraints.

Additional resources

  • Concepts
  • Resource Classes
  • Security
  • Operations
  • Machine runner 3 configuration reference

item.title: Operations
item.description:
Day-2 tasks for a running stack: the common runbooks first, then reference. Commands use the stack name runners and the shipped service names, and run on a manager node.

Task Section
See what runs, read logs Check status and logs
Add replicas Capacity and concurrency
Change the runner, proxy or images Upgrade the runner and images
Replace a class token Rotate a runner token
Restart the token proxy Restart the proxy
Patch or reboot a node Drain a node for patching

On Windows, a stop, drain or forced update of a busy container kills its job after about 5 seconds (Stop a busy Windows container).

Check status and logs

  1. List services, replicas and tasks (finished tasks stay for a short time, and the ERROR column says why a task failed or stays pending):

    docker stack services runners
docker stack ps runners --no-trunc

  2. Read a class. On Linux, entrypoint lines start with circleci-runner-entrypoint::

    docker service logs --tail 100 --follow runners_linux-default

  3. On Linux, read the distributor. Its runner-distributor: lines say which version the node installs and when the link current moves:

    docker service logs --tail 50 runners_runner-distributor

In the web app, Runners lists the replicas of each class. A name you do not recognize means someone else holds a token of that class. Healthy single-task replicas show a steady stream of tasks ending in Complete, because every finished job ends a task. Alert on:

  • Tasks that end with a non-zero exit code, including 80 and 1. Exit code 143 needs no action: a replica that gets SIGTERM while it still retries to reach CircleCI at start-up exits with 143.
  • Log lines that start with circleci-runner: error or circleci-runner-entrypoint: error, and lines with 401. In the distributor log: cannot download, SHA-256 mismatch, error.
  • Tasks that stay Pending.
  • Many tasks of one node that end within seconds: a node can stay Ready and fail every job it claims (Many jobs fail within seconds on one node).

Capacity and concurrency

The replicas of a class are the jobs it runs at once. A job with parallelism: n needs n replicas. To add replicas:

  1. Check demand. unclaimed_task_count above 0 for several minutes with every replica busy means the class is full. The API needs a personal API token (runner API reference):

    RUNNER_API=https://runner.circleci.com
CLASS=<NAMESPACE>/linux-default
curl -s -H "Circle-Token: $CIRCLECI_API_TOKEN" "$RUNNER_API/api/v3/runner/tasks?resource-class=$CLASS"

  2. Scale, then set the same replicas in your stack file, because the next deploy returns the stack to its files:

    docker service scale runners_linux-default=<REPLICAS>

  3. Check that the new replicas run. If they stay Pending, the node lacks CPU or memory for the reservations (Size the limits):

    docker service ps runners_linux-default --filter desired-state=running

Do not scale a Windows class down while it runs jobs.

Two limits sit above the replicas, both on the CircleCI side: the runner concurrency of your plan (shared by all self-hosted runner jobs of the organization) and maxConcurrentTasks of the resource class (20 by default, raised by CircleCI support). Queued tasks count against concurrency, and the inventory shows running tasks only, so runners can look idle while jobs wait. A job for a class with no runner queues indefinitely and holds concurrency: cancel it (Jobs wait while the runners are idle).

The stack has no autoscaling and no cloud integration, and a dead node is not replaced. Plan for one node less than you have. A labelled node of the token proxy carries no replicas (Where the proxy runs, and when it moves).

One token-proxy replica serves all classes of an OS, because a second would not share the list of runners that have claimed. 100 idle runners are 20 claims a second, plus the calls of running jobs. Its shipped limits are 0.5 CPU and 128 MB on Linux, 1 CPU and 512 MB on Windows. This project has not load-tested it and states no tested fleet size (the CI runs a few replicas). Before more than a few dozen replicas, test with your own load and watch docker stats --no-stream <CONTAINER> on its node, 503 answers with Retry-After in runner logs, and a rising claim count in its summary line. Raise its limits in your copy of the stack file if it is the bottleneck. A second stack (own name, proxy, classes and tokens) is the structure to try beyond that, and it is not tested.

Upgrade the runner and images

Swarm replaces containers one at a time (order: stop-first, parallelism: 1). A busy replica gets SIGTERM, drains (finishes its job, takes no new one), and is then replaced. An idle replica stops within about 5 seconds with exit code 0. A busy one exits 0 when its job ends, so an update can take as long as your longest job, up to the stop_grace_period of 5 hours and 5 minutes. docker service update waits unless you add --detach. On Windows, a stop kills a busy container after about 5 seconds.

Goal Section
Take a new release of this repository Upgrade to a new release of this repository
Change the runner version only Linux, Windows
Change the token proxy Upgrade the token proxy
Change job or base images Update the images

Upgrade to a new release of this repository

  1. Read the changelog. [BREAKING] entries say what to change.

  2. Merge the differences between your stack file and the new release. Start with the defaults of x-distributor-env: a release bumps the runner version and its MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_SHA256 values together.

  3. Record what the nodes run in deploy/deploy.env (Keep the deploy variables in version control): the new pin (both defaults merged), or your own pin with its two values. A pin, freeze or rollback made only with docker service update is not in the file, and the next deploy undoes it silently.

  4. Deploy with the same -c files and variables as before:

    sudo ./deploy/deploy.sh

  5. Check the version the distributor selected, then the active one (See what runs):

    docker service logs --tail 5 runners_runner-distributor

The entrypoint and distributor script are Swarm configs, and a config cannot change, so its name carries the first 12 hex digits of the SHA-256 of its file. A release that changes a file has new names, and the deploy updates the services that use them: runner services one replica at a time, the distributor on every node. If you edit one of these files in your own copy, rename its config after each edit (old prefix plus the first 12 digits of the new hash), or Swarm keeps the old file:

sha256sum linux/stack/circleci-runner-entrypoint | cut -c1-12
sha256sum linux/stack/runner-distributor.sh | cut -c1-12

In a clone of this repository, ci/config-names.sh --write renames the configs of the shipped stack files.

Upgrade the runner on Linux

The runner-distributor service is the only way a runner reaches a Linux node and the only place that sets its version. Runner services carry no version and no hash, so an upgrade, pin or rollback changes the distributor only: no runner service restarts and no job is interrupted (The runner distributor on Linux).

  1. On a node, read the active version (See what runs).

  2. Set the new version and its SHA-256 values in deploy/deploy.env. The default is an exact pin that each release bumps, so deploying a newer release is also an upgrade.

  3. Deploy:

    sudo ./deploy/deploy.sh

  4. Read the distributor log: it names the version it selects and each flip.

  5. Optional: replace the replicas that wait for a job now. An idle replica stops within seconds, a busy one finishes its job first:

    docker service update --force runners_linux-default

A container resolves the link current once, at start. A running job keeps its version, and the next container (next job) gets the new one. Idle replicas keep the old binary until they claim a job or exit after CIRCLECI_RUNNER_IDLE_TIMEOUT (1 hour). A persistent class runs one container for all jobs: recycle it (Recycle a class).

The version policy

The runner version is operator-pinned, as for CircleCI’s own runners. The default is an exact pin. A floating value is an opt-in.

MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION What the nodes run Changes by itself
An exact version, 3.1.13 (the default) That version: the newest the CI tests, bumped by each release (how). The stack file carries the SHA-256 of its tarballs Never. Once installed, the distributor makes no request for it
3.1 The newest 3.1.x in CircleCI’s manifest At every MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_CHECK_INTERVAL (default 24 hours)
3 The newest 3.x.y in the manifest At every check interval
current CircleCI’s current release, within MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_MAJOR (default 3) At every check interval

An exact pin takes the tarball SHA-256 from the stack file, so it asks no manifest. Once verified, each interval it only compares the active binary with its record, and reinstalls if the binary changed. A floating value reads manifest.json at start and every interval. current is matched to a versioned manifest entry by SHA-256 and adopted only within MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_MAJOR; another major logs not adopting it and keeps what is installed. A release reaches every node within one interval, with no redeploy. In a stack file, quote a floating value ("3.1"): YAML reads 3.1 as a number and 3.10 as 3.1.

Floating is weaker. A floating value cannot keep a SHA-256 list, so the distributor ignores the default list and takes each tarball’s SHA-256 from CircleCI’s manifest.json. That file comes from the same bucket as the tarball, so whoever can change one can change both, and the check proves only that the download is whole. Use it only for a class that may run whatever CircleCI releases. It can also bring a runner this release has not been tested with (Compatibility with CircleCI).

How this compares with machine runner 3, container runner and the orchestrator

CircleCI’s own runners also leave the version to you. Machine runner 3 on a host uses the OS package (apt, yum, Homebrew) or a manual install, with no auto-update. Container runner uses the image tag in the Helm values, with a floating tag per major and minor version (kubernetes-3, kubernetes-3.0) and a fixed tag per patch. The machine runner orchestrator uses the Helm chart and the pool’s disk image, whose default tag floats to the latest image (a dated tag pins it). This repository takes the container runner model: an exact pin by default, and 3.1, 3 or current to float.

Settings of the distributor

Variables of docker stack deploy, for the distributor service only. linux/stack/runners.yaml reads them in x-distributor-env.

Variable Default Effect
MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION The newest version CI tests (3.1.13 in this release) An exact version pins it. 3.1, 3 and current float (the version policy)
MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_MAJOR 3 The major version current may adopt
MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_CHECK_INTERVAL 24h How often a floating version asks the manifest again, and how often a pin’s installed copy is verified. Seconds, or a number with s, m, h or d
MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_DOWNLOAD_BASE_URL https://circleci-binary-releases.s3.amazonaws.com/circleci-runner Where manifest.json and the tarballs are (mirror). Must be https://, unless a SHA-256 list is set
MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_SHA256 The four tarball SHA-256 values of the pinned version (amd64, arm64, ppc64le, s390x) A comma-separated list for an exact pin, covering every architecture of your nodes. The distributor installs nothing else, whatever the manifest says. A version of your own needs its own values (the checksums.txt of its release) or manifest (the manifest hash is trusted: weaker). A floating value ignores any list (Runner binary integrity on Linux)
MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_ALLOW_HTTP Not set true accepts an http:// base without a SHA-256 list. For a lab: the manifest hash then protects nothing against someone on the path

The token proxy is an image, not a distributor setting (Upgrade the token proxy). The architectures are those of CircleCI’s manifest (uname -m). Another one stops the distributor with unsupported architecture.

A variable must reach every docker stack deploy, because a deploy without it sets the default again: keep them in a file. For a try, pass one with env, because sudo drops the environment:

sudo env MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION=3.1 docker stack deploy -c deploy/runners.yaml runners
sudo env MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION=3.1 linux/setup.sh --deploy --stack-file deploy/runners.yaml

Pin a version

The default is an exact pin. Pin when a runner change must go through your change process, then upgrade by changing the pin or taking a newer release. The default SHA-256 list belongs to the default pin, so a pin of your own needs its values in the same command, from the checksums.txt of that runner release, for every architecture of your nodes:

sudo env MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION=3.1.12 MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_SHA256=<SHA256_AMD64>,<SHA256_ARM64> docker stack deploy -c deploy/runners.yaml runners

Put the same two values in deploy/deploy.env. The distributor installs only a tarball with one of these values. Without the list it refuses the tarball (SHA-256 mismatch) and the nodes keep the running version. MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_SHA256=manifest trusts the manifest instead (weaker). If you edit the pin in your copy of the stack file, change both defaults together in x-distributor-env (and in x-env of microvm.yaml, which downloads the runner itself). Use 3.1.12 or later: it fixes the enforcement of max_run_time.

Freeze the nodes now. Pin the version the nodes run now (See what runs). It is installed, so no network is needed. Then put the same two values in deploy/deploy.env, or the next deploy sets the default pin again and undoes the freeze:

docker service update --env-add MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION=<VERSION> --env-add MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_SHA256=manifest runners_runner-distributor

Roll back

A rollback is a pin of an older version, with its hash policy:

docker service update --env-add MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION=<VERSION> --env-add MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_SHA256=manifest runners_runner-distributor

The distributor keeps the last 3 active versions (about 75 MB each) and never removes the active one. A rollback to a kept version only moves the link: no download, no network. A removed version is downloaded again, with its hash from the manifest or from a list you give. The file history in the volume lists the flips. The next container of every runner service runs the old version, and running jobs are unaffected. Put the same values in deploy/deploy.env, or the next deploy undoes the rollback.

See what runs 

docker service logs --tail 20 runners_runner-distributor

The volume runners_runner-bin exists on every node. On the node to inspect:

docker run --rm -v runners_runner-bin:/v:ro alpine readlink /v/current
docker run --rm -v runners_runner-bin:/v:ro alpine cat /v/history
docker top <CONTAINER_ID> | grep circleci-runner

The last command names the version directory that a container resolved at start. When a node gets no runner or a download is refused, refer to The runner waits for the distributor, and then exits with code 80.

Run the downloads from a mirror

A site without a route to CircleCI’s release bucket serves <version>/circleci-runner_linux_<arch>.tar.gz for every version the nodes may run from an internal HTTP server. The distributor builds the tarball address from the base URL and version and ignores the manifest’s url fields, so a copy of manifest.json stays unchanged.

Setting Reads manifest.json The mirror must hold
An exact pin with its SHA-256 list (the default) Never The pinned version’s tarballs, per node architecture
An exact pin of your own with manifest instead of a list Only when the version is not installed yet The tarballs, and manifest.json with an entry for that version
A floating value At every start and check interval manifest.json, kept current, and the tarballs it may pick 
base=https://circleci-binary-releases.s3.amazonaws.com/circleci-runner
mkdir -p mirror && curl -fsSL "$base/manifest.json" -o mirror/manifest.json
jq -r '.releases | keys[] | select(test("^[0-9]"))' mirror/manifest.json
for v in 3.1.12 3.1.13; do
 mkdir -p "mirror/$v"
 for arch in amd64 arm64; do
 curl -fsSL "$base/$v/circleci-runner_linux_$arch.tar.gz" -o "mirror/$v/circleci-runner_linux_$arch.tar.gz"
 done
done

Serve mirror and point the distributor at it:

sudo env MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_DOWNLOAD_BASE_URL=https://mirror.example.com/circleci-runner docker stack deploy -c deploy/runners.yaml runners

  • With an exact pin, keep the previous version too, for a rollback. With a floating version, copy its line’s versions and refresh manifest.json to let nodes adopt a release. With current, copy the version it names:

    jq -r '.releases as $r | $r.current.linux.amd64.sha256 as $s | $r | to_entries[] | select(.key | test("^[0-9]")) | select(.value.linux.amd64.sha256 == $s) | .key' mirror/manifest.json

  • The distributor uses the wget and CA bundle of the stock Alpine image, so an https mirror needs a certificate from a public authority. Otherwise use an http:// mirror with the SHA-256 list (the list, not the transport, is what you trust), or an image of your own for runner-distributor (FROM the pinned Alpine, your CA added; not tested). Do not use one proxy for both the distributor and the mirror (Proxies and certificate authorities, component by component).

  • Over plain http, an exact pin needs a usable SHA-256 list (the default one is enough), because the manifest would otherwise be the only root of trust and would travel unprotected. A floating value has no list, so it is refused. MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_ALLOW_HTTP=true accepts it for a lab.

  • The mirror replaces the runner download only. Every runner container still downloads its task agent from circleci-binary-releases.s3.amazonaws.com, and every node still pulls alpine from a registry (Does it work on hosts without internet access?).

Upgrade the runner on Windows

The service runner-distributor-windows is the only way a runner and Git reach a Windows node. It works like the Linux distributor: same variables (table), same policy, no version in the runner services. An upgrade, pin or rollback changes the distributor only, so no runner service restarts and no busy job is killed.

It installs into the volume runner-bin (versions\<version> for the runner, git\<git version> for portable Git) and mounts the links current and git\current read-only at C:\machine-runner-swarm and C:\Program Files\Git. Docker resolves a link when it creates a container, so the next job runs the new version and a running job keeps its directory. The distributor never overwrites a version or removes one in use (Windows cannot replace files a running container uses): it tries again at its next check. During a flip current is missing for a few milliseconds, and a container created then does not start (Swarm retries after the restart delay of 10 seconds). On a new node, runner tasks fail the same way until the first download is done.

Differences from Linux, in x-distributor-env of windows\stack\runners.yaml:

  • MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_SHA256 defaults to the two values (amd64, arm64) of the pinned version.
  • MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_DOWNLOAD_BASE_URL holds manifest.json and <version>/circleci-runner_windows_<arch>.tar.gz. It must be https:// (or file://), unless a SHA-256 list is set.
  • MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_TOOLS_BASE_URL is a directory URL with PortableGit-<version>-64-bit.7z.exe (arm64: -arm64.7z.exe) and 7zr.exe, the two downloads the script pins by SHA-256. Without it they come from GitHub.
  • The architecture is amd64 or arm64. CI runs the distributor on amd64 hosts only: arm64 file names and manifest entries are tested, and no Windows arm64 host runs the stack.
  • There is no start-time binary check (no entrypoint script): the distributor compares the active binary with its record at every check and reinstalls it if it changed (Runner binary integrity on Windows).
  • A mirror needs the windows tarballs, the two Git downloads in the tools directory, and manifest.json where the Linux mirror table says. The distributor downloads with PowerShell, so an https mirror needs a certificate the stock Server Core image trusts (not your own authority): otherwise use an http:// mirror with the SHA-256 list, or an image of your own. It reads only HTTPS_PROXY.

Set the variables in the shell that runs the deploy, and keep them in a file (Keep the deploy variables in version control). 3.1 trusts the manifest hash (weaker):

$env:MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION = '3.1'
docker stack deploy -c deploy\runners.yaml runners

To freeze the nodes or roll back, pin the installed or an older version (no network for a kept version; the last 3 active versions are kept), with the hash policy as on Linux:

docker service update --env-add MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION=<VERSION> --env-add MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_SHA256=manifest runners_runner-distributor-windows

docker service logs runners_runner-distributor-windows shows each flip. On the node, this shows the history and the active version:

docker run --rm --mount type=volume,source=runners_runner-bin,target=C:\v,readonly mcr.microsoft.com/windows/servercore:ltsc2022 powershell -Command "Get-Content C:\v\history; (Get-Item C:\v\current).Target"

Waiting replicas keep the old version until they claim a job or exit after CIRCLECI_RUNNER_IDLE_TIMEOUT (1 hour). A forced update replaces them at once but also kills a running job: force it only while the class is idle (docker service update --force runners_windows-default).

Upgrade the token proxy

The proxy is the image ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy, read from MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE by the service token-proxy (Windows: token-proxy-windows). Tags: X.Y.Z (a release, never moves), X.Y, X, latest (the newest release), edge (the newest main-branch commit that passed the end-to-end tests) and sha-<12 characters> (The token proxy image). A release bundle defaults to its own release by tag and digest. A checkout defaults to latest, which only a release moves.

  • With the release. Deploy the stack files of the new release (Upgrade to a new release of this repository).

  • Pin a digest. Set ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy@sha256:<DIGEST> in the environment of every deploy (deploy/deploy.env). A digest is the only pin a re-pushed tag cannot move. Read it in the release notes, in the bundle (grep MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE stack/runners.yaml), or with the command below, and check the signature first (Verify the token proxy image):

    docker buildx imagetools inspect ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy:<VERSION>

  • Change the running service. Swarm stops the old proxy before it starts the new one (a second proxy would allow a second claim). Runners cannot claim for a few seconds, and every runner that has claimed stays refused (Restart the proxy). Record the change in deploy/deploy.env, or the next deploy undoes it. A tag such as latest is resolved to a digest at deploy: deploy again to pick up a newer one.

    docker service update --image <IMAGE> runners_token-proxy

  • Roll back. Deploy the previous digest or version.

An air-gapped site mirrors the image (this keeps every platform), copies its signature with cosign copy, and sets MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE=<REGISTRY>/<NAME>:<TAG>:

docker buildx imagetools create --tag <REGISTRY>/<NAME>:<TAG> ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy:<VERSION>

Update the images

  • Stock and your own images. Change the tag or digest of image in your stack file and deploy. Swarm resolves a tag to a digest at deploy: deploy again to pick up a re-pushed tag. Rebuild your own images on a schedule (for example monthly) and when the base image or a tool changes.
  • The distributor image. runner-distributor runs alpine:3, pinned by digest. Change the digest and deploy. It restarts on every node at once, and no running job is affected.
  • Windows base images. Microsoft republishes the Server Core tags each Patch Tuesday. Pin by digest, rebuild your images on top, and change a Windows service only while its class is idle.

For one service: docker service update --image <IMAGE> runners_<SERVICE>. Record it in your stack file, or the next deploy undoes it.

Rotate a runner token

Swarm secrets are immutable: create a second secret and swap it into the service that holds the token. Single-task classes (Linux and Windows) hold it in token-proxy (Windows: token-proxy-windows), one replica, so the swap takes seconds and runners are not touched. Persistent classes hold it in the class service, which updates one replica at a time: a busy replica is replaced after its job ends (up to 5 hours and 5 minutes), so N replicas can take N times that. Raise update_config.parallelism in the stack file, or pass --update-parallelism <NUMBER> once (0 replaces every replica at once).

  1. Create a new token in CircleCI. Keep the old one until the swap is complete:

    circleci runner token create <NAMESPACE>/linux-default --nickname "linux-default-<DATE>"

  2. Create a secret with a new name, such as linux-default-token-v2:

    printf 'New token (hidden): '; stty -echo; IFS= read -r TOKEN; stty echo; echo
[ -n "$TOKEN" ] && printf 'api:\n auth_token: %s\n' "$TOKEN" | docker secret create linux-default-token-v2 -
unset TOKEN

  3. Swap the secret. Single-task class on Linux, in the proxy. Keep the target: the proxy names a class after the file <service>-token, and a new name makes a new class that no runner belongs to:

    docker service update \
 --secret-rm linux-default-token \
 --secret-add source=linux-default-token-v2,target=linux-default-token,uid=65534,gid=65534,mode=0400 \
 runners_token-proxy

    Single-task class on Windows, in token-proxy-windows (Windows secrets have no uid, gid or mode):

    docker service update `
 --secret-rm windows-default-token `
 --secret-add source=windows-default-token-v2,target=windows-default-token `
 runners_token-proxy-windows

    Persistent class on Linux, in the service (on Windows, the same without uid, gid and mode):

    docker service update \
 --secret-rm linux-persistent-token \
 --secret-add source=linux-persistent-token-v2,target=circleci_runner_config.yaml,uid=2000,gid=2000,mode=0400 \
 runners_linux-persistent

    The proxy restarts with its state from proxy-state, so only runners that have not claimed may claim. Recycle runners only when the start log says no state or state lost (Restart the proxy, and on Windows Replace refused runners on Windows), or wait for the idle timeout.

  4. Wait until the update state is completed:

    docker service inspect --format '{{.UpdateStatus.State}}' runners_token-proxy

  5. Record the new name in your stack file: source: and the entry under the top-level secrets: (for the proxy, the source: of the class under token-proxy). Otherwise a later deploy from the old file reverts the swap.

  6. Revoke the old token and remove the old secret:

    circleci runner token list --resource-class <NAMESPACE>/linux-default
circleci runner token delete <TOKEN_ID>
docker secret rm linux-default-token

If a token leaked

Do not swap first: the old token stays valid for anyone who holds it until it is deleted in CircleCI. Delete it as soon as its replacement exists.

  1. Create the new token and secret (steps 1 and 2 above). Nothing uses the secret yet.

  2. Delete the old token at once. CircleCI stops accepting it for new claims, and running jobs continue. A proxy or persistent runner that still holds the old secret fails with 401, so the class claims no new jobs until step 3 completes:

    circleci runner token list --resource-class <NAMESPACE>/linux-default
circleci runner token delete <TOKEN_ID>

  3. Swap the secret. Single-task class: in the proxy, as in step 3 above, then replace the idle runners (docker service update --force --update-parallelism 0 runners_<SERVICE>; on Windows, Replace refused runners on Windows). Persistent class: replace every replica at once. Each replica finishes its running job first. On Windows, drop uid, gid and mode, and expect a running job to end after about 5 seconds: rerun it.

    docker service update --update-parallelism 0 \
 --secret-rm linux-persistent-token \
 --secret-add source=linux-persistent-token-v2,target=circleci_runner_config.yaml,uid=2000,gid=2000,mode=0400 \
 runners_linux-persistent

  4. Do steps 4 and 5 above and remove the old secret. Then look for what the token did: unknown names in the runner inventory in CircleCI, and the jobs that ran on the class.

A leaked single-task token did not come from a job in a runner container, because those hold no token. Look at who can read Swarm secrets (the docker group on a manager), at the proxy node, and at manager backups. Rotate the tokens of every class whose secret that path reached, because the proxy holds all of them.

Restart the proxy

A restart is safe at any time, on the same node. The proxy keeps the addresses of runners that have claimed in the volume proxy-state and refuses only those afterwards. A runner that has not claimed may claim, so no restart, deploy or reboot locks a runner out.

  1. Restart (Windows: runners_token-proxy-windows):

    docker service update --force runners_token-proxy

  2. Read the start line:

    docker service logs --tail 30 runners_token-proxy

  3. state restored; <class>: N runner(s) have claimed and stay refused means you are done. no state or state lost with running tasks at CircleCI means the runners present are refused (403) until they recycle. Replace the idle ones on a Linux class:

    docker service update --force --update-parallelism 0 runners_linux-default

    A busy Linux replica finishes its job first. Do not run this on a Windows class: a busy Windows container is killed about 5 seconds after the stop, and the job with it. Use Replace refused runners on Windows.

The image does not change on restart (same tag or digest, unless the tag moved): see Upgrade the token proxy. A stop (this command, a deploy, a node shutdown) lets claims in flight finish, for 8 seconds at most, so a claim CircleCI has answered and that is saved reaches its runner. That is the Linux figure, with a Swarm grace of 10 seconds. A Windows container can be ended about 5 seconds after a stop, which can cut off a claim in flight (A claim whose outcome is unknown).

The start line names one of these states for each class:

  • state restored. All N latched addresses stay refused, also those DNS does not list yet, until DNS has not listed them for 30 seconds in a row.
  • no state (a first start) with CircleCI reports 0 running tasks. proxy-state was empty and no task of the class runs, so the runners present may claim.
  • no state (a first start) with CircleCI reports M running task(s), or CircleCI does not say how many tasks run. The proxy cannot tell which runners hold the tasks, so it fails safe and latches every runner present until Swarm replaces it.
  • state lost; ... or no state directory; .... The state file is damaged or removed, or there is no state directory: the same decision for every class, from what CircleCI says.

With no state the proxy asks CircleCI (GET /api/v3/runner/scale with each class’s token, up to three times, within 25 seconds in all). With no running task the runners present may claim. With a running task, or when the call fails, is late or answers anything else, the proxy latches every runner of that class present, so a runner that holds a job cannot claim a second one. A refused runner gets 403 until it recycles: at its idle timeout (1 hour in the shipped files) or at once with the command above.

Why 403, and not 401. Tested with the real runner 3.1.13 in single-task mode against the fake API: a 401 and a 403 on a claim behave the same. The runner keeps its container, claims again about every 5 seconds, and exits 0 only when its idle timeout ends. So replace idle runners with the command above, or use a shorter CIRCLECI_RUNNER_IDLE_TIMEOUT. A running job and a runner that starts after the proxy are unaffected.

Drain a node for patching

Restarting the Docker daemon stops every container (live restore does not work in Swarm mode), so empty the node before you patch Docker or reboot. On Linux, a drain sends SIGTERM and waits for the grace period, so running jobs finish. On Windows, a drain kills a running job after about 5 seconds: use A Windows node.

  1. Drain:

    docker node update --availability drain <NODE>

  2. Wait until no task runs on it. Swarm starts replacements elsewhere at once. If the other nodes lack capacity, they stay Pending until the drained tasks exit:

    docker node ps <NODE>

  3. Patch and reboot. Unlock a manager that uses autolock (Unlock a locked swarm).

  4. Return the node to service:

    docker node update --availability active <NODE>

Tasks do not move back by themselves, but single-task replicas restart after every job, so new tasks spread out again soon. Patch managers one at a time to keep the quorum (Managers and quorum), and the proxy node last (The node of the proxy).

A Windows node

Use pause, which keeps new tasks away and stops nothing:

docker node update --availability pause <NODE>
docker node ps <NODE> --filter desired-state=running

A running job keeps its container. Each replica that finishes exits, and Swarm starts its replacement elsewhere, so the node empties by itself. An idle replica exits only at its idle timeout (1 hour) and can claim a job until then, so the upper bound is the idle timeout plus the longest job. When the second command prints nothing, drain the node (no job is left to kill), patch it and set it active.

No unattended changes

An update that restarts the Docker daemon or the node ends every container on it (on Windows that kills jobs). On every node, switch off whatever patches or restarts without you:

  • Windows. Set the Windows Update policy to download and notify. Install and reboot only in the procedure above.
  • Debian and Ubuntu. Set Unattended-Upgrade::Automatic-Reboot "false". Hold the Docker packages, because a docker-ce upgrade restarts the daemon: sudo apt-mark hold docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io (and unhold for the planned upgrade). Set needrestart to list only: $nrconf{restart} = 'l';.
  • RHEL and its clones. Turn off automatic installation in dnf-automatic (or limit it to a download), and version-lock the Docker packages.

The node of the proxy

Draining the node that runs token-proxy stops the proxy. A proxy pinned to a labelled node stays Pending until that node is active, then starts there with its state. No claim is possible meanwhile, so choose a quiet period and patch that node last. A proxy with the default placement moves to another manager and its state stays behind (Where the proxy runs, and when it moves). Draining every manager, or the only node that can run the proxy, stops every claim: keep one node undrained for it (the warning in Multi-Node Clusters).

Stop a busy Windows container

On Linux, a stop lets the running job finish. On Windows, stopping a busy container from outside kills its job after about 5 seconds. The normal flow is unaffected: a job finishes, the runner exits, the container ends cleanly, and Swarm starts a new one.

When Docker stops a container, Windows sends it the shutdown event. The runner turns it into SIGTERM and drains, but on Server Core Windows waits only the registry value WaitToKillServiceTimeout before it ends the processes. The default is 5 seconds, whatever docker stop -t or stop_grace_period says. The container exits with code 3221225786 (0xC000013A) and the job dies with it. These stop containers this way: a rolling update (docker stack deploy, docker service update), docker service scale to a lower number, docker node update --availability drain, docker stack rm, and a restart of the Docker service. Roll out changes while the class is idle, or rerun the interrupted jobs.

Microsoft describes the limit in hcsshim pull request 1416 and Windows-Containers issue 164. It is fixed only in the containerd shim, and Swarm uses the Docker engine runtime. Test-StopHandling.ps1 measures the rule in every CI run with a fake 40 second job.

To find an idle class, use a personal API token (on CircleCI server, set $api to your runner API URL). Update or deploy when running_runner_tasks is 0:

$h = @{ 'Circle-Token' = $env:CIRCLECI_API_TOKEN }
$api = 'https://runner.circleci.com'
Invoke-RestMethod -Headers $h -Uri "$api/api/v3/runner/tasks/running?resource-class=<NAMESPACE>/windows-default"

Optional: an image that lets a job finish after a stop (DIY)

Your own image can lift the limit by setting WaitToKillServiceTimeout once, at build time, in milliseconds: at least your longest job plus a margin. This example is 18,300,000 (5 hours and 5 minutes, the runner’s max_run_time plus 5 minutes):

FROM mcr.microsoft.com/windows/servercore:ltsc2022
RUN reg add HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control /v WaitToKillServiceTimeout /t REG_SZ /d 18300000 /f

Note

Set the value at build time. Setting it at run time with reg add inside a running container does not work: Windows reads the value only when the container boots.

Use it as the image: of the service, which still mounts the runner and Git and sets PATH as in the shipped stack file. Build one image per Server Core tag, and rebuild it after each Patch Tuesday update of the base image.

Warning

Never use New-Item -Force on an existing registry key, in an image build or a running container. It replaces the key and deletes its values and subkeys. On the cexecsvc service key, the container then fails to start with hcs::System::Start: context deadline exceeded. Use reg add or Set-ItemProperty, which set one value.

This repository does not build or test such an image. Before you rely on it, run a job of a few minutes on a non-production node, force an update of its service, and check that the job finishes.

Run the cluster

Reference for production: logs that survive, signals to watch, deploy variables, backups, certificates and failures.

Ship the logs

docker service logs reads only logs of tasks Swarm still holds. Every finished job ends a task, and the task history limit of 2 makes Swarm prune old tasks, so a job log is gone after a few more jobs. The stack files keep logs on the node (local driver on Linux, 3 files of 20 MB; json-file on Windows) and rotate them.

The token proxy logs one line (about 85 bytes) per forwarded claim, a 204 included: about one per idle runner every 5 seconds. With 50 idle runners that is about 70 MB a day, so the Linux proxy’s 60 MB wrap in under a day and the Windows proxy’s 10 MB in a few hours, and the lines that matter after an incident (refused, state restored, released) are among the first lost. Before the fleet is large, ship the proxy log off the node or raise max-file of token-proxy in your copy of the stack file. To keep logs, choose one:

  • A logging driver. Change logging: in your copy of every stack file to a shipping driver such as syslog, fluentd or gelf. The stack files set the driver per service, so a default in daemon.json does not apply. docker service logs then fails for these drivers.
  • A log agent on every node. It reads container logs through the Docker API and forwards them. The stack files stay as they are, and docker service logs keeps working.

Monitor the cluster

On a manager:

docker service ls
docker node ls
docker stack ps runners --filter desired-state=running --format '{{.Name}} {{.Node}} {{.CurrentState}}' | grep -v Running

This counts, per node, the tasks that ended within the last minute or so. A node with many such tasks either fails its jobs or has more work than the others (Many jobs fail within seconds on one node):

docker stack ps runners --format '{{.Node}} {{.CurrentState}}' | grep -E ' (Complete|Failed) [0-9]+ seconds? ago' | cut -d' ' -f1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

The runner API shows what CircleCI sees (personal API token; runner.circleci.com on cloud, or your server’s runner API URL: CircleCI server, proxies, and hosts without internet). Set RUNNER_API and CLASS as in Capacity and concurrency, then:

curl -s -H "Circle-Token: $CIRCLECI_API_TOKEN" "$RUNNER_API/api/v3/runner?resource-class=$CLASS" | jq -r '.items[] | "\(.name) \(.last_connected)"'
curl -s -H "Circle-Token: $CIRCLECI_API_TOKEN" "$RUNNER_API/api/v3/runner/tasks/running?resource-class=$CLASS"
Signal Where Alert when
Replicas and nodes docker service ls, docker node ls Fewer replicas than desired for over 10 minutes (A task stays pending), a node not Ready, a manager Unreachable, or no Leader
Runners connected /api/v3/runner: items, last_connected Fewer items than replicas, or last_connected older than 2 minutes
Jobs that wait or run /api/v3/runner/tasks: unclaimed_task_count. /api/v3/runner/tasks/running: running_runner_tasks unclaimed_task_count above 0 for several minutes (concurrency). running_runner_tasks equal to the replicas for a long time: the class is full
Task exits, distributor docker service ps, docker service ps runners_runner-distributor Exit code 80, a restart loop (The container restarts every 10 seconds), fewer distributor tasks than Linux nodes, cannot download, SHA-256 mismatch, or not adopting it (current is not a version the distributor follows)
Disk df -h /var/lib/docker on every node, docker system df Above 80 percent on a worker, 70 percent on a manager (Free disk space)
Token proxy docker service ps runners_token-proxy, docker stats --no-stream on its node, its summary line Restarts, CPU near the limit, or rising refused claims (Monitor the token proxy)
A job that starts A canary job per class The canary fails, or does not start within a few minutes

A canary job runs the whole path (web app, CircleCI, proxy, node, runner), so it catches what the Swarm view does not: a healthy proxy that refuses every runner, a class whose token CircleCI rejects, and a plan with no concurrency left. It does not say which node is at fault. Run it on a schedule from a project of your own, per class:

version: 2.1
jobs:
 canary:
 machine: true
 resource_class: <NAMESPACE>/linux-default
 steps:
 - run: echo ok
workflows:
 canary:
 when:
 equal: [scheduled_pipeline, << pipeline.trigger_source >>]
 jobs:
 - canary

Monitor the token proxy

Every claim of a single-task class goes through the service token-proxy (Windows: token-proxy-windows, same log lines). It runs as one replica, and runners cannot claim without it (The token proxy).

docker service ps runners_token-proxy
docker service logs --tail 30 runners_token-proxy

GET /healthz answers 200 when every class has a usable token file. The health check is the proxy binary with -healthcheck (/machine-runner-swarm-proxy on Linux, C:\machine-runner-swarm-proxy.exe on Windows), because the images have no curl or wget. Swarm runs it every 10 seconds and restarts the task after 3 failures. A start can take up to 25 seconds before the proxy listens, so start_period is 30 seconds on Linux and 40 on Windows. The log has one line per event and never a token:

Log line Meaning
listening on :8080, upstream <host>, classes tasks.linux-default,... Started. One class per secret <service>-token it holds. A class missing here gets 403 from its runners: its secret is not mounted in token-proxy or not named <service>-token
claim from <ip> (tasks.<service>): upstream status 204 or 200 204: no task (normal, about every 5 seconds per idle runner). 200: a task was handed out, and that runner cannot claim again
released <ip> (tasks.<service>) DNS has not listed the address for 30 seconds in a row: the container is gone, and a new one on that address may claim
claim from <ip> refused: not a runner of any class (tasks.<service> lists [...], ...) Not a runner of a configured class, or one DNS does not list yet. Compare with the addresses in the line. Look for a class added without adding it to the proxy
claim from <ip> refused: this runner has already claimed a task A second claim from one container. After a restart, a runner that has claimed gets this until Swarm replaces it (Restart the proxy)
claim from <ip> refused: too many claims More than 2 claims a second from one container (429)
state: cannot write it: ... When the proxy cannot save its state
claim from <ip> (tasks.<service>): upstream status 401 CircleCI rejects the class token: deleted, or the secret holds another class’s token (The runner log shows 401)
upstream error: ... The proxy node cannot reach the runner API, or the connection broke (runners get 502). A claim that had reached CircleCI is latched (A claim whose outcome is unknown)
cannot resolve the runners, token file Swarm DNS or a class secret is unavailable (runners get 503). No latch is released meanwhile
One summary line a minute Claims forwarded, latched and refused, refusals by reason. Rising refusals while runners are healthy point to the causes above. The wording can change between releases: alert on the numbers

Limits. Each client IP gets 2 claims a second (burst 10, answer 429) and 50 requests a second (burst 200) on all paths. At most 512 requests are served at once, and one above that gets 503 with Retry-After. The proxy waits 60 seconds for CircleCI’s response headers. A runner and a job stay far below these numbers.

If the proxy is down, runners cannot claim and CircleCI keeps jobs queued. Idle runners keep polling and fail, and they cannot go around the proxy, because they hold only the placeholder. A runner that runs a job keeps its container, but its calls and its task agent’s calls to the API fail meanwhile. linux/tests/proxy.sh measures this with the real runner: a proxy restart while jobs run does not end them, and a proxy down when jobs end only delays the report (the runner sends the end of the job once the proxy is back and exits 0). The end-to-end test restarts the proxy in the middle of a real job too (probe b2). Swarm restarts a failed proxy task after 5 seconds on Linux and 10 on Windows, so an outage that short is harmless. Do not leave the proxy down long while jobs run: how long the real task agent keeps retrying is not documented.

Replace refused runners on Windows

docker service update --force replaces every container of a service at once, busy ones included, so on a Windows class it ends running jobs. A refused runner (403 this runner has already claimed a task) holds no task, so removing that one container is safe, and Swarm starts a replacement. The CI does not run these commands: check the result before you use them on a fleet.

  1. On a manager, list the addresses the proxy refused in the last minutes:

    docker service logs --since 5m runners_token-proxy-windows 2>&1 |
 ForEach-Object { "$_" } |
 Select-String 'claim from (\S+) refused: this runner has already claimed a task' |
 ForEach-Object { $_.Matches[0].Groups[1].Value } | Sort-Object -Unique

  2. On each Windows node, list the class’s containers with their addresses and find those from step 1:

    docker ps -q --filter 'name=runners_windows-default' | ForEach-Object {
 docker inspect --format '{{.Name}} {{range .NetworkSettings.Networks}}{{.IPAddress}} {{end}}' $_ }

  3. Remove only those, by name:

    docker rm -f <CONTAINER_NAME>

Or wait: a refused runner recycles at its idle timeout (1 hour). Do not shorten the timeout now: a stack file change is a service update and stops the busy containers too.

A claim whose outcome is unknown

A claim can reach CircleCI while its answer is lost: the connection resets, or CircleCI sends no response headers within 60 seconds. The proxy cannot tell whether a task was handed over, so it latches the runner (fail closed): the runner gets an error and no task, and every later claim of that container is refused (403) until Swarm replaces it. The cost is one idle runner. If CircleCI had allocated a task to it, the task never runs: rerun the job if it does not end. A claim that never reached CircleCI (the proxy cannot connect) is not latched.

When the proxy cannot save its state

The proxy saves a runner’s address before it hands the task over. If the save fails (the volume proxy-state is full, read-only or gone), that runner gets 503 and stays refused (403), every other claim gets 503 without reaching CircleCI, and the proxy deletes state.json (so no restart reads a stale state) and reports unhealthy. CircleCI has already allocated that task to the runner, which never runs it: rerun the job if it does not end. Swarm restarts the proxy after 3 failed health checks, and with the state file gone the restart asks CircleCI and refuses every runner of a class with running tasks. Mend the volume (free space, or fix the mount) before or right after: the proxy refuses to start when it cannot write its state directory.

Where the proxy runs, and when it moves

The proxy runs on a manager by default (node.role == manager), with no label. With one manager it never moves. Its state, the addresses of runners that have claimed, is the volume proxy-state of its node.

The worst case. If the proxy moves, its state is lost: the new node has an empty volume. A move happens by itself when its node is down and another manager matches, or by hand when you change the placement. The proxy then asks CircleCI for each class (Restart the proxy). With running tasks in a class, or no answer, it refuses the existing runners of that class (403) until they recycle (a runner that runs a job is unaffected). Replace the idle ones with docker service update --force --update-parallelism 0 runners_<SERVICE> per Linux class, and on Windows as in Replace refused runners on Windows. This is the safe side: no runner can claim twice.

To move the proxy by hand (if no node matches, the service stays pending and no runner can claim):

docker service update --constraint-rm 'node.role == manager' --constraint-add 'node.hostname == <NEW_MANAGER>' runners_token-proxy

Several managers, or a cluster with workers. The default lets the proxy start on any manager, and runners may share a node with it. In a cluster, label the proxy’s node and say so at deploy time (Keep the deploy variables in version control):

docker node update --label-add machine-runner-swarm.proxy=true <MANAGER>
sudo env MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_PLACEMENT='node.labels.machine-runner-swarm.proxy == true' docker stack deploy -c deploy/runners.yaml runners

The placement variable pins the proxy to a labelled node (manager or worker), and runner services never run on a labelled node, so no job shares a node with the class tokens. On a single node, with no label, the proxy and runners share the node. If the labelled node dies, the service stays pending until you label another. The labelled node runs no jobs: size the cluster so the other nodes carry the replicas.

Planned work on the proxy’s node. A reboot keeps the state, and a move loses it. If the proxy is pinned, drain the node, patch it and set it active: the proxy is pending meanwhile, no runner can claim, and running jobs wait for the proxy at the end. It then starts on the same node with its state. Keep the downtime to the patch, and patch this node last (Drain a node for patching). With the default placement and other managers, draining moves the proxy with an empty state (the worst case above): pin it first, or accept replacing the refused runners afterwards.

Keep the deploy variables in version control

The variables of docker stack deploy are the only record of your choices that the stack files do not hold: the runner pin and its SHA-256 values, the proxy image, and the proxy placement. A deploy that leaves them out silently sets the defaults again: the shipped pin, the proxy tag latest, and the placement node.role == manager (which can move the proxy to a node without its state). A docker service update change is lost the same way.

Keep the variables in a file in your own repository next to your stack files, and never deploy by hand. deploy/deploy.env (no secrets):

MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION=3.1.13
MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_SHA256=<SHA256_VALUES_COMMA_SEPARATED>
MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE=ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy@sha256:<DIGEST>
MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_PLACEMENT='node.labels.machine-runner-swarm.proxy == true'

deploy/deploy.sh, the only way to deploy on Linux (add the -c files of your add-on stack files to the last line):

#!/bin/sh
set -eu
cd "$(dirname "$0")"
set -a
. ./deploy.env
set +a
exec docker stack deploy -c runners.yaml runners

Run it with sudo ./deploy/deploy.sh: the script reads the file itself, so sudo need not keep the environment. Before the first deploy and after every edit, check that the values reach the stack. linux/setup.sh --deploy also warns when MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE is not pinned by digest.

(set -a; . deploy/deploy.env; set +a; docker stack config -c deploy/runners.yaml) | grep -E 'machine-runner-swarm.proxy ==|image: ccilabs'

On Windows, load the file into the session and deploy from it:

Get-Content deploy\deploy.env | ForEach-Object {
 if ($_ -match '^\s*([^#=\s]+)\s*=\s*(.*)$') { Set-Item -Path "env:$($Matches[1])" -Value $Matches[2].Trim("'") }
}
docker stack deploy -c deploy\runners.yaml runners

Back up the managers, and recover

The cluster state is /var/lib/docker/swarm on each manager. It holds the Raft log with every Swarm secret, so the backup holds every runner token. Keep it like a password vault and delete old copies.

The method needs a second manager: Docker stops on the manager you copy, and the others must keep the quorum. A one-manager cluster has no safe way to copy while it runs: keep your stack files and deploy variables in version control and rely on the redeploy below.

  1. If the managers use autolock, save the key: docker swarm unlock-key.

  2. Choose a manager that is not the leader (docker node ls, MANAGER STATUS) and does not run token-proxy. Use three managers so the quorum stands while one is stopped.

  3. If it runs jobs, drain it first and wait until its tasks are gone, because stopping Docker ends every container on the node (Drain a node for patching).

  4. Stop Docker, copy, start Docker, and set the node active:

    sudo systemctl stop docker
sudo tar -czf swarm-backup-$(date +%F).tar.gz -C /var/lib/docker swarm
sudo systemctl start docker
docker node update --availability active <NODE>

For this stack, disaster recovery means redeploying and issuing new tokens: the stack files hold the whole desired state, and the tokens are the only secrets.

  1. Create a new Swarm on a new manager and join the nodes (Create the swarm). Label the proxy node again.
  2. Create a new token for each class, delete the old ones, and create the secrets (Rotate a runner token). Also create runner-placeholder-token, which every runner reads in place of a token, or the deploy fails with secret not found. On Linux: printf %s machine-runner-swarm-placeholder | linux/setup.sh --secret runner-placeholder. On Windows, use the placeholder step of windows/Setup.ps1 (The token proxy).
  3. Deploy the same stack files with your deploy variables, -c files and pins. Volumes are not recovered: the proxy starts with no state and asks CircleCI, and a persistent class starts with an empty volume.

Restore the backup only to keep the node membership, or after a loss of quorum: stop Docker on the target manager, replace /var/lib/docker/swarm with the backup, start Docker, and run docker swarm init --force-new-cluster --advertise-addr <MANAGER_IP>. This makes a one-manager cluster with the old state. Unlock it if needed, check docker node ls and docker service ls, add managers and workers again, and back up again.

Unlock a locked swarm

With autolock (docker swarm update --autolock=true), a manager that restarts cannot read the Raft log until you unlock it. A locked manager answers with Swarm is encrypted and needs to be unlocked before it can be used and takes no part in the quorum. Without a quorum nothing creates replacement tasks, so rebooting managers without unlocking them drains capacity. Plan every manager reboot with its unlock.

docker swarm unlock
docker swarm unlock-key
docker swarm unlock-key --rotate

The first asks for the key on the locked manager. The second prints it, on an unlocked manager. The third makes a new key: run it after anyone who knew the old key leaves, and store the new key outside the cluster.

Rotate the cluster certificates

Swarm renews each node certificate before it expires (90 days by default). A node offline longer must leave and join again. After a node was compromised (for example a build job took over a docker-build node), remove it and rotate the CA so its certificate stops working:

docker node rm --force <NODE>
docker swarm ca --rotate

Rotate the join tokens too (docker swarm join-token --rotate worker and manager). A compromised node could read the secrets of the tasks that ran on it, and a compromised manager every secret, so also rotate those classes’ tokens (If a token leaked).

Upgrade Docker and the nodes in order

One node at a time, waiting until the cluster is healthy before the next. Managers first, then workers, and the proxy’s node last (docker service ps runners_token-proxy; Windows: runners_token-proxy-windows). With three managers, one is down at most, so the quorum holds.

  1. Drain the node (Drain a node for patching). On Windows, pause it and wait instead.
  2. Upgrade Docker and reboot. Unlock a manager that uses autolock.
  3. Return it to service (docker node update --availability active <NODE>). docker node ls must show it Ready, and a manager Reachable or Leader.
  4. After the proxy node, check the proxy log: the start line must say state restored. no state means the proxy moved or lost its volume, and runners are refused until they recycle (Restart the proxy).

Leave mixed Docker versions only for the length of the upgrade. The runner upgrades separately, with no stop.

Node death

Swarm marks a node Down after it misses its heartbeats and starts replacement tasks on other nodes that match the constraints.

  • The jobs on the node are lost. CircleCI reports them as failed because of a problem with your infrastructure. Self-hosted runners have no automatic retry: rerun the workflow from the failed job.
  • Services pinned to the node stay Pending: the persistent class (node.hostname) and the docker-build classes (a labelled node). Capacity drops by the node’s replicas until it returns or other nodes have room.
  • A returning node rejoins by itself while its certificate is valid. Swarm does not move tasks back.
  • A node gone for good: docker node rm --force <NODE>. For a lost manager use docker node demote (if reachable) or docker node rm --force, and add a new manager to hold the quorum. The cluster runs while a majority of managers remains. Without one, running jobs finish but no replica is replaced (Managers and quorum).

Recycle a class

A forced update replaces every replica of a service one at a time, each with a runner drain. Use it to move a persistent class to a new runner version, or to reset it. On Windows, recycle a class only while it is idle (Stop a busy Windows container).

docker service update --force runners_linux-persistent

Recycling removes only the container filesystem. The named volume survives, so /home/circleci (Linux) and C:\cache (Windows) keep their files. To reset the volume too, scale the service to 0, run docker volume rm runners_persistent-home (Linux) or docker volume rm runners_windows-persistent-cache (Windows) on the node that holds it, and scale back up.

On Linux, a persistent class does not clean its working directory: the runner user cannot remove files the job user owns, so the stack sets CIRCLECI_RUNNER_CLEANUP_WORK_DIR to "false". Start every job on that class with a step that removes what an earlier job left, and recycle the class on a schedule (Working directory cleanup).

Free disk space

A full disk is the most common way a node stops running jobs, and a full manager disk can break Swarm itself.

Where the space goes

  • Stopped containers. A job runs in its container’s writable layer, which stays until Swarm prunes the task. A slot keeps its running task and up to task-history-limit finished ones (Swarm’s default is 5), so R replicas can hold R times (1 plus the limit) layers. A job that leaves gigabytes behind makes this the largest item.
  • Images. Every tag a job image has had, and every version of your own images, stays until something removes it. docker image prune removes only untagged images.
  • Logs: 3 files of 20 MB (60 MB) per runner on both systems and for the Linux proxy, 10 MB for the Windows proxy. A docker-build node’s engine: images, volumes and build cache that jobs leave. Raft log and Swarm state, in /var/lib/docker/swarm of each manager.

Prevent it

  1. Set the task history limit. docker swarm update --task-history-limit 2 keeps at most 2 finished tasks per slot. The single-node setup of linux/setup.sh sets it. A swarm you create yourself does not (Create the swarm).

  2. Give Docker its own filesystem, and keep managers free of jobs. Put /var/lib/docker on a separate volume, sized for the worst case above: replicas, times the largest workspace, times (1 plus the history limit), plus images. A manager with the proxy label runs no jobs.

  3. Prune images on every node, on a schedule. Swarm has no command that runs on every node, and a global service with the Docker socket would be root everywhere, so use each node’s scheduler (configuration management, or a systemd timer on Linux). Create /etc/systemd/system/docker-image-prune.service, which removes images no container uses that are older than a week:

    [Unit]
Description=Remove unused Docker images older than a week

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/bin/docker image prune --all --force --filter until=168h

    Create /etc/systemd/system/docker-image-prune.timer, which runs it every Sunday:

    [Unit]
Description=Weekly removal of unused Docker images

[Timer]
OnCalendar=Sun 03:00
RandomizedDelaySec=1h
Persistent=true

[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target
    sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable --now docker-image-prune.timer

    until filters by image creation time, not last use, and --all skips every image a container (stopped ones too) still uses. A removed image that is needed again is pulled again, so a mirror (What needs the internet) must be up. On a docker-build node, add docker builder prune --force --filter until=168h. On Windows, run the same docker image prune from a scheduled task. The Server Core and distributor images are in use while the stack runs, so a prune keeps them.

  4. Alert on every node’s disk (df -h /var/lib/docker): above 80 percent on a worker, 70 percent on a manager (Monitor the cluster).

Warning

Do not run docker volume prune or docker system prune --volumes on a node of this stack. The named volumes hold runner-bin, proxy-state and the persistent classes. A volume no container uses at that moment (for example a persistent class scaled to 0) is deleted with its data. Leave docker container prune to the task history too, except in an emergency.

When the disk is full

A node with a full disk fails tasks, with no space left on device in the runner log or in docker stack ps --no-trunc, and Docker commands on it fail. A full manager disk comes first, because Swarm cannot write its log.

  1. Find the node: df -h /var/lib/docker on each, and the ERROR column of docker stack ps runners --no-trunc.

  2. Stop it from claiming jobs. On Linux, drain it. On Windows, pause it (A Windows node):

    docker node update --availability drain <NODE>

  3. See what takes the space:

    docker system df
docker ps -a --size --format '{{.Size}}\t{{.Names}}' | sort -hr | head

  4. Free it, cheapest first. docker container prune removes the stopped containers of finished tasks (Swarm does not need them) and no running one. Do not prune volumes:

    docker image prune --all --force
docker builder prune --force
docker container prune --force

  5. If the disk is a manager, check that docker node ls and docker service ls answer and the proxy runs (docker service ps runners_token-proxy).

  6. Return the node to service (docker node update --availability active <NODE>), set the task history limit if it is not set, and add the scheduled prune.

Compatibility with CircleCI

The token proxy sits between the runner and CircleCI, so it depends on the runner API more closely than a plain runner install.

What the proxy relies on

Call Who sends it What the proxy does, and reads
POST /api/v3/runner/claim A runner The only call the proxy changes. It accepts the claim from a runner address that Swarm DNS lists for a class, adds that class’s token, and forwards it. A 2xx other than 204 means CircleCI handed a task over: the proxy latches that runner. 204 means no task. Any other status passes through, nothing latched
GET /api/v3/runner/scale The proxy, with a class token, at a start with no state for the class It reads data.attributes.running_task_count and data.attributes.unclaimed_task_count, each a whole number of 0 or more. Anything else is an error, and the proxy latches the runners present
Every other call The runner and task agent Forwarded unchanged with the caller’s own token (the placeholder, for the runner). The proxy relies on the runner passing CIRCLECI_RUNNER_API_URL on to its task agent, so these calls go through it too

The claim and scale calls are the runner’s internal protocol, not in CircleCI’s public runner API reference. CircleCI does not promise they stay as they are.

What is tested

  • The runner version. The exact pin of the stack files, 3.1.13 in this release. The CI runs the real runner binary against a fake API (task.sh, proxy.sh and others), and the end-to-end jobs run real jobs on CircleCI cloud through the proxy, on Linux amd64 and arm64 and Windows Server 2022 and 2025. The distributor test also installs the previous version (3.1.11) for the rollback, and the version CircleCI names as current in the live manifest, and checks its record.
  • Not tested. A real job on a floating version (3.1, 3, current) or any runner version other than the pin. CircleCI server. A runner API on a host other than runner.circleci.com.
  • The task agent is not pinned by this project: the runner downloads the version CircleCI serves, at each container start.

What fails when it changes

Change What you see What to do
The claim moves to another path The runner logs 401, and the proxy log has no claim from lines for it: the call is forwarded with the placeholder, and CircleCI rejects it Pin the previous runner version (Roll back)
A claim with no task gets a 2xx other than 204 Each runner is latched after its first poll: upstream status 200, then this runner has already claimed a task. No runner claims Pin the previous version, and replace the runners (Restart the proxy)
scale answers in another shape A proxy that starts with no state logs CircleCI does not say how many tasks run and refuses the runners present until they recycle. A proxy with state is unaffected Open an issue with the log line. Replace the runners, or wait for the idle timeout
The runner stops passing its API URL to the task agent, or the agent calls another host The job starts and its steps fail with 401 against CircleCI Pin the previous runner version

Before you move to an untested runner version (any floating value included), pin it on one class, run the canary and a real job, read the proxy log, and keep the previous version installed so the rollback needs no network. The runner API hosts nodes must reach are in Egress hosts, with their source, CircleCI’s runner FAQ.

CircleCI server, proxies, and hosts without internet

Two setups are not tested yet: CircleCI server, and an installation with no route to the internet. Nothing here promises either works.

  • CircleCI server. The proxy takes the runner API address in its -upstream argument, in the command of token-proxy in the stack file. The CI runs against CircleCI cloud and a fake API, never a server installation. Open questions: whether the claim and scale calls match your server version, which runner versions your server accepts (the default pin is tested against cloud only), and whether the proxy and runner trust your server’s certificate (the table below). Run the canary first, and do not assume anything on this page was checked for your version.
  • An air-gapped installation. It does not work with this release: every runner container downloads its task agent from circleci-binary-releases.s3.amazonaws.com at start, and no setting redirects that. Nodes must reach that host, directly or through a proxy the runner honours.

What needs the internet

Needed by Host When Mirror here?
The token proxy (claims), and the runner and task agent (their calls go through it) runner.circleci.com, or your server’s runner API Always No: it is the API
Every runner container (task agent) circleci-binary-releases.s3.amazonaws.com At every container start No
The runner distributor The same host At first install and at an upgrade. With a floating version, at every check interval. With the default pin, never once installed Yes: MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_DOWNLOAD_BASE_URL (mirror)
The Windows distributor github.com: PortableGit and 7-Zip When it installs a version of Git Yes: MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_TOOLS_BASE_URL
The jobs circleci-tasks-prod.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com (cache, workspaces, artifacts), your VCS provider, whatever the job commands fetch During a job Not part of this project
Docker on each node The registries of the image: lines: Docker Hub for alpine, ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy and job images, and the Windows base image registry At a deploy, when a node joins, when an image changes Yes: copy the images to your registry and change image:
The MicroVM install github.com: the Kata tarball At install Yes: copy the tarball in (MicroVM)
Verifying a release or image The Sigstore services cosign uses When you verify See Verify a release without internet

To mirror the images, copy each with its digest to a registry the nodes reach (this keeps every platform), and change the image: line of every stack file and MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE. Deploy with --resolve-image never if the manager cannot reach the registry to resolve tags (Registry needs):

docker buildx imagetools create --tag <REGISTRY>/<NAME>:<TAG> <SOURCE_IMAGE>

Proxies and certificate authorities, component by component
