op["Operator creates the Swarm secret<br/>a runner config file with auth_token"]
raft["Swarm managers<br/>encrypted Raft log"]
proxy["token-proxy container<br/>single-task classes<br/>Linux: uid 65534, mode 0400<br/>Windows: administrators only"]
file["Secret file in the runner container<br/>Linux persistent class: uid 2000, mode 0400<br/>Windows persistent class: administrators only"]
runner["circleci-runner<br/>single-task: a placeholder token and the proxy as API URL"]
api["runner.circleci.com"]
job["Job steps<br/>no token in the environment"]
cli -- "shown once" --> op
op --> raft
raft -- "mutual TLS, only to nodes that run the task" --> proxy
raft -- "mutual TLS, only to nodes that run the task" --> file
runner -- "every API call, the claim carries the placeholder" --> proxy
proxy -- "HTTPS, adds the class token to the claim only" --> api
file --> runner
runner -- "HTTPS, the token authenticates the runner" --> api
runner -- "task agent runs the job as the job user" --> job
job -. "persistent class: Linux with the sudo opt-in, Windows always" .-> file

A single-task class (Linux and Windows) takes the path through the proxy: only the proxy holds the class token. A persistent class takes the direct path: the runner holds the token itself.

Linux

  • Single-task classes. The class secret <service>-token is mounted into the token-proxy service and nowhere else. Runners read a placeholder config, so the sudo setting does not decide whether a job reaches the class token.
  • Storage. A class secret is a minimal runner config file with only api.auth_token. Swarm mounts it as a read-only file in memory: in the proxy container at /run/secrets/<service>-token (uid 65534, mode 0400), or, in a persistent class, in the runner container at /run/secrets/circleci_runner_config.yaml (owner circleci-runner, uid 2000, mode 0400). Every other runner mounts the placeholder secret runner-placeholder-token at the same path. The token is in no environment variable, no command line, and no stack file, and docker inspect does not show it.
  • Users. The runner runs as circleci-runner, which has no sudo rights and cannot write to /opt/machine-runner-swarm. Jobs run as the job user, stepped down with command_prefix.
  • Default class. The job user keeps passwordless sudo, so a job is root in its container. It can read the placeholder and the files of the runner, and become the runner user, but finds no class token. It still gets the task token of its own job.
  • Hardened class. MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO: "false" steps every job down with setpriv --no-new-privs, even when the image has sudo, and the container does not start when the image has no util-linux setpriv. Swarm ignores no-new-privileges, so this per-job flag, inherited by everything the job starts, is what stops a setuid binary (sudo, su, or one with a local-root bug) from lifting a job to root. The job gets none of the CIRCLECI_RUNNER_* and MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_* variables, cannot read the file or the process of the runner, and cannot become another user. Tools must be in the image. A kernel or container-runtime bug can still lift a job to root. Use it for shared or regulated work. Users and the runner token on Linux compares the classes.

linux/tests/token.sh measures these probes against the real runner binary, with a sentinel token in the runner’s config file as the persistent class has it. linux/tests/proxy.sh scans the files, /proc/*/environ and /proc/*/cmdline of the runners as root and finds no class token.

Probe, run as the job user Default class Hardened class
Read the config file (the real token in the persistent class, the placeholder in the others) Denied Denied
Read /proc/<runner pid>/environ, or find the token in the job environment Denied, no token in it Denied, no token in it
sudo -n true Works Fails: NoNewPrivs stops the setuid sudo
Run a setuid-root binary through the step-down of the runner Becomes root Stays the job user: NoNewPrivs is 1. Without the flag the same binary reads the token
Write to /opt/machine-runner-swarm No No

Windows

  • Single-task classes. The class secret <service>-token is mounted into the service token-proxy-windows and nowhere else. Runners read a placeholder, as on Linux.
  • Storage and users. Swarm places the secret at C:\ProgramData\Docker\secrets\<target>. Windows has no uid, gid, or mode for secrets, and only administrators and SYSTEM can read the file. There is no step-down: the runner and the jobs run as ContainerAdministrator, because the runner needs its symbolic link privilege. A job can read the config file of its runner (the placeholder, or the token in a persistent class). The token is not in the job environment.
  • No NET_RAW drop. The proxy uses the source address to tell the runners of a class apart, and a Windows container cannot drop NET_RAW, so a job can forge a source address. This gains little: the answer to a claim goes to the owner of the address, and a container that has claimed cannot claim again. Windows is not tested for this.
  • Clear text on disk. Swarm writes the secret as plain text to the root disk of the proxy container (and of the runner container, in a persistent class) until the container stops. Linux keeps it in memory (tmpfs). Anyone who can read the Docker root directory of the host can read a Windows token, so enable BitLocker.
  • The proxy is not a boundary against a hostile job on its host. A job runs as an administrator, with process isolation, next to the proxy when both run on one node. Microsoft does not treat process isolation as a security boundary. It becomes a boundary only when the proxy runs on a node that runs no jobs (label that node machine-runner-swarm.proxy=true) and untrusted classes run with Hyper-V isolation, which needs nested virtualization on a virtual machine and is not tested here. The end-to-end jobs on Windows run real jobs through the proxy, but only record whether a job can read the token and assert nothing about it, and no test forges a source address. Treat these protections as untested, and use one trust group of classes for each host.

Treat each Windows resource class as a trust boundary. Use one token for each class and host, restrict who can use the class, and rotate tokens.

Swarm

  • Swarm stores secrets encrypted in the Raft log of the managers, and sends a secret only to nodes that run a task that uses it.
  • Optionally lock the managers with docker swarm update --autolock=true. It protects the secrets at rest, but each manager then needs docker swarm unlock after every Docker daemon restart.
  • Keep join tokens private, and rotate them with docker swarm join-token --rotate.
  • A user in the docker group on a manager can read every token. Limit administrator access to the managers.

The token proxy

The service token-proxy in runners.yaml keeps the class tokens of the single-task classes away from the runner containers and their jobs. One proxy serves every class of the stack, and docker-build.yaml and ssh-rerun.yaml add their classes to it. Concepts shows how the pieces fit.

What it does

  • Only the claim gets the class token. The proxy replaces the Authorization header of the task-claim call (POST /api/v3/runner/claim) with the class token and passes every other call on unchanged. The runner and its task agent use the task token from the claim response, which is scoped to one task.
  • The network decides the class, not the caller. Every secret <service>-token in its secrets directory is the class <service>, whose runners are tasks.<service>. runner-placeholder-token is never a class, and no runner token is mounted into the proxy. A claim is allowed only from an IP address that Swarm DNS lists now for tasks.<service>, and gets the token of that class. Any other address (a container that you started on the class network, or an address that two classes list) gets 403 and nothing reaches CircleCI. The 403 says only claim refused: the reason is in the log of the proxy, where a job cannot read it.
  • One claim per container. After a claim that returns a task, that address cannot claim again until DNS has not listed it for 30 seconds in a row, which means the container is gone. One missing answer, even a no such host for the whole class, is one poll of the 30 and never a release.
  • A job cannot forge the source address on Linux. The proxy attaches to each class overlay with endpoint_mode: dnsrr, so it sees the address of the container that connects. The runner services drop NET_RAW, so even root in a container cannot send packets with another address. Keep cap_drop: [NET_RAW, MKNOD] or ALL on every class that uses the proxy.
    • The encrypted class networks need Docker Engine 23.0.3 or later (or 20.10.24). Earlier engines accepted unauthenticated VXLAN traffic on encrypted overlay networks (CVE-2023-28840), which lets a host on the node network inject packets into a class overlay. The setup helper requires Docker 24 or later.
    • The exception is linux-microvm-docker, which cannot drop NET_RAW (BuildKit needs it). It runs in a VM with no NET_ADMIN, stays at one replica, and has an overlay of its own, so no other runner of its class exists to impersonate (MicroVM jobs).
  • It remembers who has claimed, also after a restart. It writes the addresses that have claimed to the volume proxy-state before the runner gets its task. If it cannot write them, the claim fails, and the proxy removes the state file (and keeps its marker), so the next start takes the fail-safe path below.
    • A restart with a state refuses every address in it, and only those.
    • A start with no state (an empty proxy-state, a lost state, a new class) does not guess. For each class the proxy asks CircleCI how many tasks run (GET /api/v3/runner/scale, with the token of that class). With none running, the runners present may claim. With some running, or when the call fails, it refuses every runner of that class present until Swarm replaces it.
    • The state stays on the node. If the proxy moves, it starts empty there: Where the proxy runs, and when it moves.
  • An unknown outcome counts as a claim. When the request reached CircleCI but the answer was lost (a timeout, a broken connection), the proxy latches the runner as if the claim had succeeded, so that runner is refused until Swarm replaces it. This costs a runner, never a second task for one container. It waits at most 60 seconds for the response headers of the upstream.
  • It fails closed. It does not start without a usable token file for every class, nor when it cannot write its state, and it answers 503 when DNS fails, a token file disappears or it cannot write its state. A count of running tasks that CircleCI does not give as a whole number of 0 or more (data.attributes.running_task_count and unclaimed_task_count, exactly these names), or does not give in 25 seconds for all classes together, counts as running tasks. It logs addresses, class names, and status codes, never a token.
  • It limits what a job can send it. A claim is accepted from one address at most twice a second, with bursts of 10, and its body is at most 64 KiB. Every client address is limited to 50 requests a second, with bursts of 200, and the proxy serves at most 512 requests at once: more get a 503 with a Retry-After header. These limits are not proof against a hostile job: a job that sends enough requests from the containers of its class can use up the 512 shared slots and the one replica, and the claims of every class then wait. The proxy logs one summary line a minute (Monitor the token proxy).
  • It is small. One static Go binary in a distroless image (no shell), uid 65534, no capabilities, a read-only root filesystem, no published port. Its secrets are the class tokens and nothing else. The image is signed (The token proxy image).

What it does not do

  • It sees the runner traffic of its classes. Claims, task configuration and step output pass through it over plain HTTP on the overlay network. The class token is never on that path, but the task token is. Between nodes, the Linux class networks are encrypted by default (IPsec, which needs IP protocol 50 (ESP) open: Encrypted class networks). Docker does not support encrypted overlay networks for Windows containers, so Windows class traffic is plain between nodes: keep those nodes on a network that you trust.
  • It is one point of failure. One replica serves all classes, because a second replica would not share the record of who has claimed. While it is down, no runner can claim, and a running job keeps its container while its calls wait (Monitor the token proxy).
  • Its node holds every class token. A job that escapes its container onto that node reads them. The proxy never runs on a Docker-build node or on a node of the container agent, which holds the Docker socket. It runs on a manager by default. In a cluster, label the node machine-runner-swarm.proxy=true and pin the proxy to it with MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_PLACEMENT: runner services never run on a node with that label. On a single node there is no such label, and jobs run next to the proxy.
  • It depends on the runner API. It knows two calls, POST /api/v3/runner/claim and GET /api/v3/runner/scale, tested against the runner version that this release pins. If CircleCI changes them, the proxy fails closed and jobs wait until a release follows the change. Pin the runner version in production. This page makes no claim about how the Runner Terms apply to a proxy between your runners and CircleCI: that is for your own review.
  • It does not cover the persistent classes (The persistent class), and it does not replace CircleCI-side controls: a stolen class token still lets its holder run a runner on that class (CircleCI-side controls).

Windows runs its own proxy, token-proxy-windows (the windows/amd64 image of the same tag), because a Windows node does not share its network with a Linux proxy. It works as described here, with the differences in Windows. There is no windows/arm64 image (Windows).

The persistent class

A persistent class (persistent.yaml) does not use the proxy. A continuous runner claims a task after every job, and the proxy allows one claim for each container, so the runner keeps its token in a file in its own container. This class is weaker than the proxied classes:

  • The shipped file sets MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO: "false", so the token file is unreadable to the job user, and the tools that jobs need must be in the image. With the opt-in "true", a job that uses sudo reads the class token and can run a runner of its own on that class.
  • State from one job is visible to the next, because the container lives on.

Give the persistent class a resource class of its own, restrict it to trusted projects with a config policy, keep production contexts away from it, and rotate its token on a schedule. See Persistent mode.

Runner binary integrity on Linux

The runner executes your jobs, so it must be the binary that CircleCI published. The runner-distributor service installs it and the entrypoint checks it before every start (The runner distributor on Linux).

Where the runner comes from

The distributor downloads the tarball over HTTPS from the release bucket of CircleCI and compares its SHA-256 with the values that the stack file carries for the pinned version (MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_SHA256: amd64, arm64, ppc64le and s390x). Each release of this repository bumps the version and these values together, copied from CircleCI’s manifest. This is trust on first use from the same bucket: CircleCI publishes no signature for the runner that this stack checks. A later change of the bucket cannot change what the nodes install.

  • Floating versions are weaker. A floating value (3.1, 3, current) has no list, because the version is not known in advance. The distributor ignores the default list and compares the SHA-256 with CircleCI’s manifest.json. The manifest comes from the same bucket as the tarball, so whoever can change one can change the other: the check proves that the download is whole, not that CircleCI published it. It is the same trust as the runner’s own download of the task agent.
  • An exact version of your own needs its own list, from the checksums.txt of its release (every architecture of your nodes), or the word manifest. The distributor then installs only a tarball that matches.
  • A mirror (MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_DOWNLOAD_BASE_URL) must be an https:// URL unless a usable SHA-256 list is set for an exact pin: over plain http the manifest, and with it the hash, could be changed on the way. A floating value has no list, so an http:// base is refused unless MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_ALLOW_HTTP=true. The microVM classes download the runner into every VM with the same rules.

The checks

When Who What
Download and install Distributor The SHA-256 of the tarball must equal a value of the list (or, with manifest, the manifest value), otherwise nothing is installed. The binary must report exactly the version that it installs (a pin of 3.1.1 does not accept 3.1.13). The SHA-256 of the binary goes to versions/<version>/SHA256. Files are owned by root
Every check interval (24 hours by default) Distributor It compares the active binary with its record, and installs the version again when the binary changed
Every container start Entrypoint It resolves current once and runs sha256sum -c against the record. A missing record or a different binary ends in exit code 80 and the log line does not match its SHA-256 record (Error: does not match its SHA-256 record). Hashing the 74 MB binary takes about 0.05 seconds
While a job runs Mount The volume is read-only in the runner containers (files owned by root, mode 0755). The entrypoint is an immutable Swarm config

The token proxy image

The distributor does not install the token proxy. It is the image ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy of Docker Hub, which Swarm pulls, and its integrity rests on the image digest.

  • A release bundle names the image by tag and digest (ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy:<version>@sha256:<digest>), so Docker pulls exactly the image that the release pipeline pushed, whatever happens to the tag later.
  • A checkout names the tag latest, which only a release moves and which is not a digest. Pin a digest for anything that matters (Upgrade the token proxy). linux/setup.sh --deploy warns when MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE is not pinned by digest.
  • ccilabs is the Docker Hub organization of CircleCI Labs. You trust the signature below, not the name: an image of that name that does not verify is not this project’s.

Every digest that the pipeline pushes is signed, and the pipeline checks the signature again before it gives the image its release tags. The Linux index (four platforms), each Windows image (Server 2022 and 2025) and the manifest list that joins them are signed separately. The image runs as the user 65534 (Windows: ContainerAdministrator), and the state of the proxy is the only thing it writes.

Verify the token proxy image

The signature is a keyless cosign signature, made with the OIDC token of the CircleCI job that pushed the image, like the signature of a release (Verify a release). It proves that a job of this CircleCI project pushed that digest. Verify the digest that you run, before you run it. You need cosign 3.1.3 or a later 3.x (CI signs and verifies with 3.1.3, and earlier versions are not tested). A digest of the manifest list covers every platform. Pass the tag, and cosign resolves it to the digest and prints it.

cosign verify ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy:<VERSION> \
 --certificate-identity "https://circleci.com/api/v2/projects/7bbdbb66-6ba8-4f6c-982e-d4fb401ec257/pipeline-definitions/8b2a66db-3f28-5c80-88e4-03f4694b5b60" \
 --certificate-oidc-issuer "https://oidc.circleci.com"

The command prints the verified claims as JSON when the project and the pipeline definition above signed the image. Compare the digest in its output with the one in your stack file. A tag from a commit that is not a release (edge, sha-<12 characters>) verifies the same way.

This is only the signature check. It does not look at the ref, and the identity does not name a branch, so a job of any branch can sign with it. A reader who stops here accepts an image that a job of any branch signed. The ref check is a second, separate step: the extension 1.3.6.1.4.1.57264.1.14 must be refs/heads/main in every signature of the digest. cosign has no flag for that extension, so this command reads it, with the same pattern as Verify a release (the OID, then the value refs/heads/main, from a byte boundary):

cosign download signature ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy:<VERSION> \
 | jq -r '.verificationMaterial | (.certificate // .x509CertificateChain.certificates[0]).rawBytes' \
 | while read -r cert; do printf '%s' "$cert" | base64 -d | od -An -v -tx1 | tr -d ' \n' \
 | grep -Eq '^([0-9a-f]{2})*2b0601040183bf30010e0411(0c|13)0f726566732f68656164732f6d61696e' \
 || { echo "NOT signed for refs/heads/main: do not use this image"; exit 1; }; done && echo "every signature is for refs/heads/main"

The notes of every release name the image of that release.

What remains

  • Not verified: the task agent, which every container downloads from the same bucket at start, with no pin and no check (it runs as the job user and holds the task token), and the source of the pinned SHA-256 values (CircleCI’s manifest at the time of the bump).
  • A race at start. The check narrows the window and does not close it: a sibling that rewrites the file between the hash and the exec of one container start is not detected.
  • A privileged sibling container with SYS_ADMIN on the same node could mount the volume read-write and change both the binary and its record. The docker-build class mounts the Docker socket and can do the same (Docker Builds). The microVM classes do not mount the volume: each VM downloads and verifies its own runner (MicroVM jobs).
  • Whoever can update the runner-distributor service (for example a user in the docker group of a manager) chooses the version and the download address. A list in MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_SHA256 limits what can be installed to the tarballs on it.

Runner binary integrity on Windows

The trust is the one of Linux. The service runner-distributor-windows downloads the tarball over HTTPS from the release bucket of CircleCI, compares its SHA-256 with the two values (amd64 and arm64) that the stack file carries for the pinned version, checks that the binary reports the version, and records its SHA-256 in versions\<version>\SHA256. A floating value ignores the list and uses CircleCI’s manifest.json (weaker), and a mirror must be https:// unless a usable list is set for an exact pin (or MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_ALLOW_HTTP=true when there is no list). Portable Git and 7zr.exe are pinned by SHA-256 in the script, so a new Git version is a new release of this repository.

Two things differ from Linux:

  • The runner is the main process of the container and there is no entrypoint, so nothing checks the binary when a container starts. The distributor compares the active binary with its record at every check interval (24 hours by default) and installs it again when it changed.
  • A job runs as an administrator in its own container, and the volume is mounted read-only through two links, so a job cannot change the runner or Git. A container with write access to the volume can, for example one of the docker-build class (Docker Builds).

Compared with the official runner installs

The first three columns are our reading of the public CircleCI documentation as of 17 October 2026. They are not statements by CircleCI, the pages change, and the sources below are the reference. The last two columns come from the tests of this repository. Where the public documentation says nothing, the cell says so.

Machine runner 3 package Container runner Machine runner orchestrator This repository, default class This repository, hardened class
Can a job read the class token? A job gains the privileges of the task agent, and the runner runs as the same user (circleci) Not stated. The agent holds the tokens in a Kubernetes secret No: a sidecar keeps the token out of the VM No, even with sudo: the token proxy holds it. A job that escapes onto the node of the proxy could read it No, for the same reason. The persistent class is the exception (The persistent class)
Can jobs use sudo? Whatever you grant the circleci user Set by the job image and the pod securityContext No by default (grantSudo: false) Yes, passwordless, as in the Docker executor No: the step-down uses setpriv --no-new-privs
Boundary between jobs None: each job runs on the machine where the runner is installed An ephemeral pod, on the shared node kernel A virtual machine for each job A new container for each job, on a shared kernel The same

Sources: Self-hosted runner concepts, Self-hosted runner overview, Container runner reference, and the Machine runner orchestrator reference, including its sidecar and grantSudo.

  • A clean container is not a virtual machine. The orchestrator is the only column with a hardware-level boundary between jobs. If jobs must not share a kernel, use the orchestrator, or dedicate nodes to one trust group (Why Swarm and not container runner or another runner?).
  • The token. The single-task classes here work like the orchestrator’s sidecar, except that a job that escapes onto the node of the proxy reaches the tokens. The persistent class and Windows are weaker: the token is a file in the container (Windows). The Windows persistent class is at parity with the official Windows runner, and the Windows classes have no hardened variant.

Hardening defaults

Linux defaults

Settings in linux/stack/runners.yaml. Tokens, the proxy and the runner volume are covered above.

Control Setting
Users The runner user has no sudo. The job user is stepped down. The entrypoint is a Swarm config with mode 0555
Working directory CIRCLECI_RUNNER_CLEANUP_WORK_DIR: "false" (Working directory cleanup)
Filesystem and logs The root filesystem is writable, and /tmp is writable and executable. Text logs, the local driver, 20 MB for each of 3 files
Shutdown init: true, and stop_grace_period: 5h5m so that a running job finishes
Capabilities Default classes drop NET_RAW and MKNOD. The hardened class drops all and adds back CHOWN and FOWNER (the entrypoint sets the owner of directories), SETUID and SETGID (the step-down), KILL (the init process signals the runner, which has another uid), and AUDIT_WRITE (sudo audit messages)
Limits pids: 4096, nofile 65536, no core dumps, and reservations that equal the limits
Network One overlay network for each class, no published ports, so SSH rerun is off unless you deploy the SSH add-on stack file
Runner version 3.1.12 or later. The default pin is the newest version that this repository’s CI tests

Swarm ignores security_opt, privileged, userns_mode, and the short tmpfs form, and its tmpfs mounts are not executable. The stack therefore sets no no-new-privileges and no read_only filesystem for the runners. The default seccomp and AppArmor profiles of Docker apply.

Keep the host clock on NTP, because TLS fails silently when the clock drifts. Keep SELinux or AppArmor enforcing on the node. Disable swap, or size memory knowing that Swarm cannot set a swap limit.

Working directory cleanup

On Linux, the stack files and the entrypoint set CIRCLECI_RUNNER_CLEANUP_WORK_DIR: "false". The runner (uid 2000) cannot remove files that the job user owns, so with cleanup on every task fails before it starts, with failed to remove working directory before starting task and permission denied. Running jobs as the runner user would give every job the runner token and remove the step-down.

  • Single-task classes. Nothing is lost: Swarm discards the container after the job.
  • Persistent classes. Nothing removes what a job leaves, and the next job can read it. Start every job with a step that removes what an earlier job left, and recycle the class on a schedule (Persistent mode).

Do not set the variable to true on Linux (Error: failed to remove working directory). On Windows the jobs and the runner use the same account, so cleanup stays on.

Windows defaults

Settings in windows\stack\runners.yaml:

  • The runner and Git are read-only mounts of the volume runner-bin (current at C:\machine-runner-swarm, git\current at C:\Program Files\Git), and the secret is readable by administrators and SYSTEM only.
  • CIRCLECI_RUNNER_CLEANUP_WORK_DIR: "true". Logs use the json-file driver with rotation.
  • stop_grace_period: 5h5m, but a stop from outside kills a busy container after about 5 seconds, so change a service while its class is idle (Stop a busy Windows container).
  • CPU and memory limits. The Windows engine rejects pids and ulimits. init, cap_drop, read_only, and tmpfs have no effect.
  • No published ports, so SSH rerun is off unless you deploy the SSH add-on stack file.

Isolation between runners

Replicas of one class share an overlay network and can reach each other. Swarm cannot prevent this: enable_icc=false is ignored on swarm-scoped networks, and a stack cannot use a node-local bridge network.

  • Linux. Each class has its own overlay network, so classes cannot reach each other. Containers can still reach the host network and the internet through default egress.
  • Windows. The overlay is the only network option. All Windows classes share one overlay network, and it is not encrypted, so Windows classes can reach each other, and their traffic is in clear text between nodes (Encrypted class networks).

To reduce the exposure:

  • Run sensitive classes on dedicated nodes (Multi-Node Clusters).
  • Filter egress on the host, for example in the DOCKER-USER chain on Linux. Docker bypasses ufw and firewalld rules for published ports and for container traffic.
  • Rely on single-use containers: a compromised replica disappears with its job.
  • Any container on a class network can reach the proxy. It answers only claims from the runners of the class.

Cloud nodes: block the metadata address

Nothing in this stack or in Docker stops a job from reaching the instance-metadata service that cloud providers serve at 169.254.169.254. On a cloud VM, it can hand out the credentials of the role attached to the node and, on some clouds, the user data of the instance. A job that reads them acts as the node. This is true of every self-hosted runner on a cloud VM.

These recipes are the usual ones, and they are not tested in this repository’s CI. Check them on your own nodes with a job that runs curl -m 3 http://169.254.169.254/, which must fail.

  1. Give the node role the fewest permissions that the node needs, often none. Do not leave the Swarm join token readable in the user data or startup script of an instance: a job that reaches the metadata service reads it, and with it joins a node to your Swarm.

  2. Block the address for containers on Linux. Add a rule to the DOCKER-USER chain, which Docker evaluates before its own rules for container traffic:

    sudo iptables -I DOCKER-USER -d 169.254.169.254 -j DROP

    Docker creates the chain when it starts, so add the rule after Docker is up, and again after a reboot. This systemd unit starts after docker.service and adds the rule only when it is missing:

    [Unit]
Description=Block the instance metadata address for containers
After=docker.service
Requires=docker.service

[Service]
Type=oneshot
RemainAfterExit=yes
ExecStart=/bin/sh -c 'iptables -C DOCKER-USER -d 169.254.169.254 -j DROP 2>/dev/null || iptables -I DOCKER-USER -d 169.254.169.254 -j DROP'

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

    The rule does not cover a container on the host network (the docker-build class can use one) or the host itself. Check it with sudo iptables -S DOCKER-USER after a reboot and after a restart of Docker. If your Docker uses another firewall backend, use its equivalent.

  3. On AWS, require IMDSv2 and a hop limit of 1. This disables IMDSv1 and stops the session-token response from reaching a container behind Docker’s bridge or NAT:

    aws ec2 modify-instance-metadata-options --instance-id <INSTANCE_ID> --http-tokens required --http-put-response-hop-limit 1 --http-endpoint enabled

    It does not cover containers on the host network. It also breaks every job that uses the node role through the metadata service: give such jobs their credentials another way, for example through a context or OIDC.

  4. On other clouds, allow the metadata service from the host only, and attach a role with minimal permissions. On Windows nodes these settings apply too, but have not been tried with Windows containers.

Listening ports on a node

The stack publishes no other port, and the token proxy publishes none.

Port Protocol Nodes Used for Who may reach it
2377 TCP Managers Cluster management The nodes of the cluster only
7946 TCP and UDP All Node discovery The nodes of the cluster only
4789 UDP All Overlay network (VXLAN) The nodes of the cluster only, even though the Linux class networks are encrypted: an unfiltered port lets a host on the network send packets to the overlay
IP protocol 50 (ESP) All IPsec of the encrypted Linux class networks (Encrypted class networks) The nodes of the cluster only
53 TCP and UDP Every node, with the routing mesh The DNS forwarder microvm-dns of the microVM classes. It is an open resolver for anyone who can reach the node The nodes of the cluster only
54782 TCP The node that runs a task of the SSH class Rerun job with SSH The networks where your users connect, such as a VPN

Docker publishes the last two ports with NAT rules that run before ufw and firewalld rules, so a rule in either does not restrict them. Filter them in the DOCKER-USER chain or with a cloud security group. This example, not tested here, drops port 54782 from sources outside a VPN range:

sudo iptables -I DOCKER-USER ! -s <VPN_RANGE> -p tcp --dport 54782 -j DROP

Inter-node ports has the rules for the cluster ports.

CircleCI-side controls

The stack cannot decide which projects may use a class. Apply these controls in your organization.

  1. One class and one token for each service. Give each token a nickname that names its host or purpose, so you can revoke it alone. Only organization admins create and delete resource classes. Delete the tokens of a class before the class.

  2. Config policies. Restrict each class to named projects with the resource_class_by_project helper. Config policies need the Scale plan on cloud, or server version 4.2 or later. A class that is not in the mapping stays available to every project.

    package org
import data.circleci.config

policy_name["runner_policies"]

enable_hard["resource_class_check"]

resource_class_check = config.resource_class_by_project({
 "<namespace>/linux-hardened": {"<project ID>"},
 "<namespace>/linux-docker-build": {"<project ID>", "<project ID>"}
})

    Enable evaluation and push the policy (Config policies for self-hosted runner):

    circleci policy settings set --org <ORG> --enabled
circleci policy push ./config-policies --org <ORG>

  3. Context restrictions. Project restrictions, security groups, and expression restrictions combine with logical AND. Restrict every context that jobs on a runner class use. For deploy contexts, add an expression such as pipeline.git.branch == "main" and not job.ssh.enabled.

  4. No fork builds on public projects. CircleCI does not make self-hosted runners available to public projects that have Build forked pull requests enabled.

  5. SSH rerun stays off unless a class needs it. The shipped classes leave CIRCLECI_RUNNER_SSH_ADVERTISE_ADDR unset and publish no ports. If you deploy the SSH add-on stack file, keep its class for named projects and restrict inbound port 54782 with the DOCKER-USER chain or a cloud security group (Rerun job with SSH).

  6. Monitoring. Watch the runner inventory for names you do not know, and the logs for 401 and for exit code 80. In the log of the token proxy, a refused claim comes from a container that is not a runner of a class, or from a runner that tries to claim twice (Monitor the token proxy).

Runner classes are usable only by jobs of the organization that owns them.

Egress hosts

Runners need outbound HTTPS only, and no inbound access. Allow these hosts by name, because their addresses change.

Host Port Used for
runner.circleci.com 443 The runner API. With the token proxy, only the node of the proxy calls it for the single-task classes
circleci-binary-releases.s3.amazonaws.com 443 The task agent, which every new container downloads, and the runner download (by runner-distributor, runner-distributor-windows, or each container of a microVM class)
circleci-tasks-prod.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com 443 Caches, workspaces, artifacts, and test results
internal.circleci.com 443 Not on CircleCI’s list of hosts for self-hosted runners (the two hosts above, the cache host, and your VCS host). Allow it only if a job log shows that a step needs it
Your VCS host, for example github.com 443, and 22 for SSH checkouts Checkout. For Bitbucket Cloud over SSH, CircleCI’s changelog says the agent uses ssh.bitbucket.org from 12 November 2026
Your image registries, for example Docker Hub and mcr.microsoft.com 443 Pulling the service images, on Linux also the alpine image of runner-distributor. The token proxy image comes from Docker Hub (registry-1.docker.io, auth.docker.io and its content delivery network), or from a mirror that you name with MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_PROXY_IMAGE
github.com and release-assets.githubusercontent.com 443 On Windows, Git for Windows and 7-Zip, which runner-distributor-windows downloads (not in an air-gapped setup with a mirror). The first host redirects the downloads to the second

If your VCS organization uses an IP allow list, add the egress addresses of your nodes. If you use an explicit proxy, test a checkout through it before you roll out a class. Jobs inherit HTTPS_PROXY and NO_PROXY from the service environment in the stack file.

What needs internet

The stack accepts no inbound connection. Only CircleCI cloud with internet access is tested. A host without internet access, and CircleCI server, are not tested in this release. Egress hosts lists the hosts. What fetches what:

Part Fetched by Cloud Server
The release bundle, SHA256SUMS and signature (once, on any host) You, from github.com. cosign also downloads the Sigstore trust root on first use (tuf-repo-cdn.sigstore.dev). Not tested offline Needed Needed
The stack images, and Git and 7-Zip on Windows Docker and the Windows distributor, from your registries and github.com. A mirror can replace each Needed, or a mirror Needed, or a mirror
The runner The distributors, and each container of a microVM class Needed, or a mirror Not tested
The task agent Every new container at start (CircleCI’s runner downloads it) Needed Not tested
The runner API The token proxy, for claims Needed Your server host: set -upstream of the proxy
Jobs Checkout, caches, workspaces, artifacts, test results, and whatever the job fetches Needed The storage of your server, not tested

Mirrors replace the downloads of this stack, and do not replace the task agent: see Run the downloads from a mirror and Upgrade the token proxy. CircleCI lists three hosts for machine runners in its runner FAQ: runner.circleci.com, circleci-binary-releases.s3.amazonaws.com and circleci-tasks-prod.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com. The other hosts come from this stack.

CircleCI server

CircleCI documents machine runner 3 for server 4.4 and later, and says that an install on server sets the API URL of the runner (CIRCLECI_RUNNER_API_URL, or api.url in the config file). This repository is tested against CircleCI cloud only. Here the runners call the token proxy, so the URL of your server goes to the -upstream argument of the token-proxy service (its command in the stack file), and the runners keep CIRCLECI_RUNNER_API_URL: http://token-proxy:8080. Whether the proxy and the runner download work against your server version is not known, and no job of this project has run against one. Config policies need the Scale plan on cloud or server 4.2 or later.

BitLocker on Windows hosts

Docker keeps a Swarm secret in clear text on the container root disk until the container stops. Encrypt the volume that holds the Docker root directory (C:\ProgramData\docker by default) with BitLocker, and confirm the protection status:

Get-BitLockerVolume

The status of the volume must show that protection is on. BitLocker protects the token when someone steals the disk, or a snapshot or backup of it. It does not protect against a job, or an administrator who is logged in to the live host, because both read the decrypted file. Limit the local administrators of the host, use one token for each class and host, and rotate tokens. See the Microsoft documentation for BitLocker on Windows Server for the setup steps, including the recovery key.

item.title: FAQ
item.description:
What is this repository?

Docker Swarm stack files, a Linux entrypoint, a service that keeps the runner on every node, optional setup helpers, and documentation. Together they run CircleCI machine runner 3 in containers, with one resource class for each Swarm service and a new container for every job. Refer to Concepts.

Does CircleCI support it?

No. It is part of CircleCI Labs, a pre-release 0.x project, and CircleCI support does not cover it. Field engineering handles issues on a best-effort basis. Your normal CircleCI support covers the runner itself, the platform, and your resource classes. What is tested says how each claim is checked, and which are not.

What must I build?

Nothing, with one optional exception on Windows. Swarm pulls one published image, the token proxy (ccilabs/machine-runner-swarm-proxy), and the release bundle names it by digest.

Needs Optional
Linux A Docker engine and a Swarm join. The runner-distributor service fills a per-node volume with the runner, and a stock image such as cimg/base runs it A custom image when jobs need tools (it needs util-linux setpriv). Refer to Images
Windows A Docker engine, the ltsc2022 base image, and a Swarm join. The runner-distributor-windows service installs the runner and portable Git into a volume A custom image, and a DIY image that lets a job finish after a stop. Refer to Windows images and the stop-timeout image

What do sudo -niHu and setpriv mean?

They are the two forms of the runner command_prefix, which makes a job run as another user (reference). The entrypoint sets it in every Linux container, and the service environment cannot override it.

  • sudo -niHu circleci -- is the default class: never prompt, login shell, HOME of the target user, run as circleci. /etc/sudoers.d/90-circleci-runner allows only the runner user (uid 2000), and only to the job user.
  • setpriv (util-linux) switches to the job user and clears every capability. The hardened class always uses it with --no-new-privs, so sudo, su or a setuid binary cannot lift a job to root. An image with no sudo uses it too.

MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_JOB_SUDO chooses between the two classes (Users and the runner token on Linux).

Should I use the setup helper or the manual steps?

Either. Both give the same result, and every helper step is on the install pages (Linux, Windows). A rerun is safe.

  • The helper does: check the node, create a single-node Swarm, create secrets from hidden prompts, and deploy the stack files you name. On Windows it also labels the node with the image tags it can run.
  • It does not: install Docker or the runner (the distributor does), create classes or tokens, edit the stack file, label or join other nodes, or build images.

Why Swarm and not container runner or another runner?

Choose by what you already run and the isolation you need.

You have or need Use
Elastic capacity, nothing to host CircleCI cloud executors
Kubernetes, jobs that fit a docker: executor Container runner
A boundary stronger than a container, privileged or KVM jobs, a full OS, autoscaling Machine runner orchestrator: a VM for each job on Kubernetes with KubeVirt, and the token stays out of the VM (comparison)
One host or a few, jobs that need the whole machine Machine runner 3 on a host: the simplest setup, nothing separates one job from the next
The same, in a container Machine runner 3 on Docker: the container is reused, so the environment is not clean
Docker hosts or Windows containers, no Kubernetes, a clean container for every job This repository: replicas, placement, secrets and rolling updates. No CircleCI support, no autoscaling, no node creation, and containers share the host kernel

The stack files use only core Swarm features. To move to the orchestrator or a plain machine runner later, keep the resource class names, and jobs with machine: true stay as they are. Container runner needs jobs that use a docker: executor.

The microVM add-on runs each job in a Kata Containers microVM on Swarm nodes with KVM. It is experimental: CI runs the real runner against a fake CircleCI API on nested virtualization on AWS (amd64), and no real CircleCI job, other cloud, or arm64 is tested in CI. One real CircleCI job ran by hand on a Kata Cloud Hypervisor class. If you need a hardware boundary today, use the orchestrator.

Why not plain Docker Compose?

Compose restarts the same container, so files outside the working directory survive into the next job. Swarm creates a new task and container for every job, keeps the token in a Swarm secret instead of an environment file visible in docker inspect, and adds many nodes with placement, rolling updates and drain. The price is Swarm concepts, even on one node.

linux/tests/ephemerality.sh has a negative control: three jobs on docker run --restart always ran in one container, and two found files from an earlier job. To move off the old docker-compose.yml, refer to Migrate from Docker Compose.

Is Docker Swarm a safe bet?

The project can state what it checks, and cannot promise the future of Swarm.

  • What it uses. Core Swarm features only: services, secrets, configs, overlay networks, placement constraints, rolling updates.
  • Docker versions. CI runs Docker 29.4.2 on Linux and 29.4.0 on Windows. The documented minimum is 24 on Linux and 28.0 on Windows (Linux, Windows).
  • The way out. Resource class names are CircleCI objects, so jobs with machine: true keep their class when you move it (alternatives).
  • Support. CircleCI Labs, 0.x, best effort, no commitment on how long it is maintained.

Does it support macOS?

No. Docker has no macOS containers, so Swarm cannot schedule macOS jobs. CircleCI documents machine runner 3 on a Mac directly, and offers hosted macOS executors.

Which operating systems does it support?

Platform Status
Linux, Ubuntu LTS, amd64 Tested in CI, including real jobs
Linux, Ubuntu LTS, arm64 Every pipeline tests that the distributor installs the runner and that the stack starts. On main and smr-swarm/* branches, three probe jobs also run on a real arm64 runner
Linux, ppc64le and s390x The distributor and token proxy are built for them. CI emulates them under QEMU: the distributor installs the runner of the right architecture, and the token proxy image runs. Nothing else runs there
Linux, RHEL 8 and later Steps documented, not tested in CI
Windows Server 2025 and 2022 Tested in CI, on amd64
Windows on arm64 The distributor is built for it. The token proxy has no windows/arm64 image (Windows). No arm64 host runs the stack in CI
Windows Server 2019 Supported by machine runner 3. Untested here, and the stack files have no label for it
Windows Server 2016 and older Not compatible with machine runner 3
macOS Out of scope

Which CircleCI plans and platforms work?

CircleCI cloud, on Linux and Windows. CircleCI server is not tested. To try server, change the -upstream argument of the token-proxy service to your server URL and keep CIRCLECI_RUNNER_API_URL: http://token-proxy:8080 on the runners (CircleCI server).

Self-hosted runners need at least one credit on your account, although runner compute does not use credits (Run jobs on self-hosted runners). Their concurrency is separate from hosted jobs and shared by every class of the organization (see the Runner tab). Config policies, which restrict classes to projects, need the Scale plan on cloud or server 4.2 or later (Config policy management overview).

How do I scale up or down, and see how many jobs wait?

Swarm has no autoscaling, so you choose the number of replicas.

  • Permanent. Edit deploy.replicas in your stack file and deploy again with the same files (Choose replica counts). To go beyond one node, add nodes (Multi-Node Clusters).

  • Quick. docker service scale runners_linux-default=4. The next docker stack deploy resets it. A scale-down stops containers: on Linux a running job finishes first, and on Windows it is killed (why).

  • Queue depth. Ask the runner API with a personal API token, not a resource class token:

    curl -s -H "Circle-Token: $CIRCLECI_API_TOKEN" "https://runner.circleci.com/api/v3/runner/tasks?resource-class=<NAMESPACE>/linux-default"
curl -s -H "Circle-Token: $CIRCLECI_API_TOKEN" "https://runner.circleci.com/api/v3/runner/tasks/running?resource-class=<NAMESPACE>/linux-default"

    The first prints {"unclaimed_task_count": 3}, the second {"running_runner_tasks": 2}. Jobs wait while unclaimed_task_count stays above 0 and every replica is busy. Raise the replicas by that number if the nodes have room (Monitor the cluster).

Does it scale to zero, and what does idle capacity cost?

No. Capacity is fixed and you pay for the peak: an idle replica keeps its reserved CPU and memory on nodes that you run. Scale to zero is a manual replicas: 0, and a class with no runner queues jobs without limit and holds concurrency (Capacity and concurrency). Which replica a scale-down removes is not documented, and a scale-down while jobs run is not tested: assume it can remove a busy one (on Windows it kills the job). For elastic capacity, use the machine runner orchestrator or CircleCI cloud executors.

Does it create or remove nodes?

No. You install Docker, join the node to the Swarm, and label it from a manager (a node cannot label itself), and a Windows node needs its base image before the first task. A terminated instance leaves a Down node until you run docker node rm. There is no cloud integration or machine image. If you create nodes with user data, do not leave the Swarm join token readable in it (Cloud nodes: block the metadata address). Refer to Multi-Node Clusters.

Where are the tokens kept, and can I use my secrets manager?

Class tokens are Swarm secrets. There is no integration with an external secrets manager. Anyone in the docker group on a manager can read every token, and a Windows secret is stored in clear text on the disk of the proxy container (Token model on each OS). Rotation is manual and not tested in CI (Rotate a runner token).

What is not in this release?

  • Autoscaling and creation of nodes.
  • Metrics export (Monitor the cluster).
  • An external secrets manager, and a tested rotation of tokens.
  • A hardened Windows class, and Hyper-V isolation.
  • CircleCI server and hosts without internet access: neither is tested (What needs internet).
  • A one-command verification script. Use the commands of Verify a release.

Is there a delay between jobs?

About 10 seconds for the restart delay, plus container start and the task agent download, before a replica claims the next job. Other replicas keep working meanwhile. Refer to Job lifecycle.

Do I need to open inbound ports?

No. Runners connect outbound over HTTPS, and the shipped classes publish no ports. Only the optional SSH add-on publishes port 54782 (Rerun job with SSH). Multi-node clusters need the Swarm ports between nodes (Inter-node ports).

Can I run a long-lived runner with warm caches?

Yes, with a persistent class. It gives up the clean environment, so use it only for trusted projects. The shipped Linux persistent class gives jobs no sudo by default. Refer to Persistent mode.

Can it run Docker executor jobs?

As a prototype, yes. The classes of this repository run jobs with machine: true. Container mode adds a Swarm service on each opted-in Linux node that runs jobs with a docker: list and its service containers, as container runner does on Kubernetes. It has no SSH reruns and no Docker layer caching, and it has not yet run against the real CircleCI API. A resource class serves one mode, so give container mode its own classes and tokens. For production Docker executor jobs today, use container runner.

Can I use Rerun job with SSH?

Yes, with the add-on file ssh-rerun.yaml, which defines linux-default-ssh (windows-default-ssh on Windows). A rerun uses the class of the original job, so the job to debug must run on that class. It is experimental: the Swarm side was proven by hand, no CI test logs in over SSH, and the Windows file is untested. Refer to Rerun job with SSH.

Can a job read the runner token?

Not in a single-task class, with or without sudo: the runner container holds only a made-up placeholder, and the token proxy holds the class token. On Windows no test asserts this, and a hostile job on the same host as the proxy can reach the token, because process isolation is not a security boundary (Windows). In a persistent class the container holds the token: on Linux a job that uses sudo can read it (the shipped class disables sudo), and on Windows every job can. Use BitLocker and one token for each class and host. A holder of a token can run a rogue runner on that class, so rotate tokens (how). Refer to Token model on each OS.

What is the token proxy, and what happens when it is down?

The service token-proxy (token-proxy-windows on Windows) holds the class tokens so that runner containers and jobs never do. Runners hold a placeholder and send their API calls to the proxy, which adds the real token to the task claim, once for each container. Persistent classes do not use it. Refer to The token proxy and Security.

When it is down, no runner can claim and jobs wait in CircleCI. Idle runners fail their claims and retry, and Swarm restarts a failed proxy after 5 seconds. A running job keeps its container, but its API calls (step output) also go through the proxy, so keep outages to a restart. A claim whose outcome is unknown is latched like a successful claim: that runner is refused until Swarm replaces it, so the proxy fails closed.

  • Placement. The proxy runs on a manager by default. In a cluster, label its node machine-runner-swarm.proxy=true: runner services never run there (Where the proxy runs, and when it moves).
  • Limits. Each client address gets 50 requests a second (bursts of 200), and the proxy serves at most 512 requests at once.
  • Monitoring. Monitor the token proxy.

Why does a Windows job end when I update or stop a service?

Stopping a busy stock Server Core container from outside kills its job after about 5 seconds, whatever stop_grace_period says. Change services while the class is idle, or rerun the interrupted jobs. Refer to Stop a busy Windows container.

Which runner version do the nodes run?

The runner-distributor service decides. The default is an exact pin, with the tarball SHA-256 values in the stack file: the newest runner version that CI tests, bumped by each release. Nodes keep it until you change it. To float, set MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_RUNNER_VERSION to 3.1, 3 or current. Floating is weaker: the distributor trusts the manifest hash, and a newer runner can change the protocol that the proxy depends on, so the proxy fails closed and jobs wait. Pin an exact version in production. runner-distributor-windows works the same way. Refer to The version policy and Upgrade the runner on Windows.

How does the runner version policy compare with machine runner 3, container runner and the orchestrator?

It follows them: machine runner 3 on a host has no auto-update, container runner and the orchestrator take the image tag from Helm values, and here it is a setting of the distributor, an exact pin by default. Refer to How this compares.

How do I verify a release?

Each release has a SHA256SUMS file and a keyless cosign signature made with the CircleCI OIDC token. Run the single check block on Verify a release (or on Windows): it prints RELEASE VERIFIED only when the signature, the ref (refs/heads/main) and the checksums all pass. The runner binary is a separate download: the distributor verifies its SHA-256, and on Linux the entrypoint checks it at every container start (Runner binary integrity on Linux).

Can a fork pull request use these runners?

No. CircleCI does not make self-hosted runners available to a public project that has Build forked pull requests enabled. Keep that setting off for any project that uses these classes. For a private project, a collaborator’s branch runs your code on the node, so restrict each class to the projects that need it (CircleCI-side controls).

Which jobs cannot run here?

Jobs run in unprivileged containers on a shared kernel, so some belong on another runner.

Job needs Here Use instead
A privileged container, /dev/kvm, or host devices No. Swarm ignores privileged and devices. The microVM add-on gives a job its own kernel, not host devices The orchestrator, or a machine runner on a host
Docker-in-Docker, setup_remote_docker, or Docker commands in a job No, except in the opt-in docker-build class, which is root-equivalent on its node The docker-build class, a daemonless builder, or a daemon in the VM of the microVM add-on
A GPU Not supported or tested A machine runner on a GPU host
A docker: executor job, or service containers Only in container mode, a prototype, in classes of its own Container mode, or container runner
Desktop or UI automation on Windows No. Windows jobs are headless A machine runner on a host

Do proxies and custom certificate authorities work?

The stack sets nothing for them, and this repository does not test them.

  • Proxy. Set HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY and NO_PROXY under environment of the service. Jobs inherit them. On Linux, also set HTTPS_PROXY on token-proxy, which calls runner.circleci.com for the runners, and add NO_PROXY: token-proxy to the runners. Test a checkout through the proxy before you roll out a class (Egress hosts).
  • Certificate authority. Add your CA to a custom image and run update-ca-certificates, or mount a CA bundle read-only and point SSL_CERT_FILE at it. Windows images need the CA in the image. On Linux, the token proxy needs the CA too when a proxy or your CircleCI server uses it: mount the bundle into token-proxy and set SSL_CERT_FILE there (Images).

Does it work on hosts without internet access?

No, and it is not tested. Every runner needs outbound HTTPS to runner.circleci.com, and every new container downloads the task agent from circleci-binary-releases.s3.amazonaws.com. A host that reaches those names through an allow list or a proxy works. On Linux the distributor download can come from your own mirror: set MACHINE_RUNNER_SWARM_DOWNLOAD_BASE_URL (Run the downloads from a mirror). The mirror does not replace the task agent download, and the images must come from a registry the nodes reach (Registry needs). What needs internet lists every download.

Does it work with rootless Docker, user namespaces, or Podman?

  • Podman cannot run Swarm, so it cannot run this stack.
  • Rootless Docker and userns-remap are not tested. The stack assumes a root daemon: the entrypoint checks that the runner volume belongs to root, and the secret belongs to uid 2000. Swarm also ignores userns_mode in stack files.

Does it work with SELinux on RHEL?

The RHEL steps are documented and not tested in CI. Keep SELinux enforcing. The runner is in a Docker volume, so no host directory needs a label. For a denial, refer to Troubleshooting.

What happens to a job when a node dies?

The job is lost. CircleCI reports an infrastructure failure, and self-hosted runners do not retry, so rerun it. Swarm starts replacement runners on other matching nodes. A single manager that dies stops all replacements (Managers and quorum). Refer to Node death.

How do I report a bug or a vulnerability?

Open a GitHub issue for a bug. For a vulnerability, email security@circleci.com (SECURITY.md).
